Following the election of Donald Trump as the US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. With the new US administration taking office, the direction of US policies may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have profound implications for the global economic landscape. Notably, risks facing emerging market economies have intensified amid a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, a stronger US dollar, and the potential adoption of trade protectionist measures by the US. The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate remained broadly stable, while HKD Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) rose in tandem with their US dollar counterparts. Nevertheless, liquidity conditions remained sound, and overall loan growth picked up further in the second half of 2016. Following the introduction of the new stamp duty measure, the residential property market showed signs of adjustment immediately, but has rebounded recently. Looking ahead, banks should carefully assess the impact of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes and broader US policy uncertainties, particularly the risk of massive capital outflows and the potential implications for domestic interest rates. Following the election of Donald Trump as the US President, the global economy faces greater uncertainty. Not only was the election outcome unexpected by the market, but the subsequent market reactions were also surprising. In particular, expectations that Trump's proposed tax reforms, increased infrastructure spending, and deregulation would boost US economic growth have driven global stock markets higher. With the new US administration taking office, the direction of US policies may undergo fundamental changes in two aspects — from monetary easing to fiscal expansion, and from globalisation to anti-globalisation — which could have profound implications for the global economic landscape. However, the market-anticipated tax cuts by Trump may fail to produce the expected stimulus effect on US economic growth. Especially as US economic activity is currently operating close to its economic potential, fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth, but would exacerbate the upside risks to US inflation. While it remains uncertain whether the US Federal Reserve (the Fed) will significantly accelerate the pace of monetary policy tightening as a result, long-term bond yields have already risen notably, partly reflecting market expectations of increasing inflation risks. At the same time, the rise of trade protectionism would result in a "lose-lose" situation for both the US and the rest of the world. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm overall interests, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Meanwhile, political instability remains a major risk and headwind, particularly for the European economy where the recovery remains fragile. For emerging market economies, the risk of capital outflows has increased due to the faster pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar. This could drag down economic growth and exacerbate the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, driven by expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration and concerns over surging energy prices, the market has repriced inflation risks, leading to a broad-based and significant rise in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Box 1 (see page 13) assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. The findings show that since the "taper tantrum" in 2013, the impact of the US Treasury bond market on sovereign bond markets has deepened, and US interest rate hikes and tightening financial conditions will have a significant impact on both advanced and emerging market economies. In East Asia, economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016 alongside a rebound in exports, but the earlier market volatility—characterised by regional currency depreciation and rising sovereign bond yields due to concerns over potential policy changes by the new US administration—only gradually stabilised early this year. Looking ahead, East Asia may maintain stable growth in 2017, but the risks and uncertainties it faces have both increased. US interest rate hikes, regional currency depreciation, and heightened financial market volatility may lead to a tightening of financial conditions. At the same time, the US may pursue protectionist policies, which could affect economies in the region, although the actual impact remains unclear at present. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated marginally in the second half of 2016, supported by resilient growth in infrastructure investment and an improvement in private sector business spending. Although the economy continues to show signs of stabilisation, uncertainties remain over the Mainland's growth outlook. In particular, given the government's determination to curb rising housing prices, the real estate sector's contribution to growth may decline this year if the property market continues to cool. Meanwhile, the ongoing economic structural adjustments and changes in Sino-US trade relations may increase uncertainties surrounding the short-term economic outlook. On the external front, although the renminbi (RMB) remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressures increased towards the end of 2016 amid a stronger US dollar and US interest rate hikes, before appearing to ease slightly in early 2017. Despite signs of stabilisation in private sector economic activity, there are still some market concerns about the effectiveness of monetary policy, especially given that M1 growth has accelerated while M2 growth has slowed. Box 2 (see page 24) explores whether the Mainland economy has fallen into a liquidity trap, while Box 3 (see page 27) examines the factors that may have led to the divergence between M1 and M2 growth. The findings suggest that there is no evidence indicating the Mainland has fallen into a liquidity trap, and the main reasons for M1 growing significantly faster than M2 are that monetary easing in recent years has lowered the opportunity cost of holding liquid money, and rising economic uncertainty may have increased the precautionary demand for money. Hong Kong's economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Quarter-on-quarter real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth rose from 0.8% in the third quarter to 1.2% in the fourth quarter. Domestically, private consumption growth continued to strengthen, while robust infrastructure activity in the fourth quarter drove investment growth. Externally, goods export growth picked up alongside improving regional trade flows, while exports of services grew steadily in tandem with the recovery in trade-related and transportation services. Due to faster growth in imports of goods and services, net exports continued to drag on real GDP growth in the second half of the year. With the pick-up in economic growth, the overall unemployment rate edged down to 3.3% in December. Economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. The Government's and the market consensus forecasts for real GDP growth in 2017 are 2-3% and 2.0% respectively. However, Hong Kong's growth outlook still faces significant external headwinds. The protectionist rhetoric of the new US administration has increased the downside risks to global trade and Hong Kong's external demand. Amid appreciation pressures on the US dollar and expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, the global financial environment is expected to provide less support to the real economy, and could lead to a tightening of domestic financial conditions, particularly if tail risks materialise. Box 4 (see page 41) discusses the compilation of a Financial Conditions Index for Hong Kong to help monitor domestic financial conditions. Domestic inflationary pressures have remained moderate since the second half of 2016, while quarter-on-quarter inflation momentum picked up slightly in the fourth quarter of 2016, mainly driven by volatile food prices and rising housing rentals. With stable import prices and mild domestic cost pressures, inflationary pressures are expected to remain contained. Despite market volatility, the HKD exchange rate remained broadly stable, though it occasionally weakened following the US interest rate hike in December. The Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. Along with the appreciation of the US dollar, the nominal effective exchange rate of the HKD rose further. Due to the large Monetary Base, HIBORs remained at low levels, but have risen since October driven by year-end funding demand and catching up with US interest rate hikes. Consequently, the average mortgage rate, after falling to a recent low of 1.71% in October amid intense competition in the mortgage lending business, edged up to 2.07% in January 2017. Overall loan growth accelerated to 4.2% in the second half of 2016, compared with a growth of 2.2% in the first half. The growth was supported by stronger domestic economic activity and increased funding demand from multinational corporations towards the year-end. Domestic loan growth picked up slightly, while loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded after a small decline in the first half of the year. Analysed by currency, HKD loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half of the year, while foreign currency loans recorded a growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced the repayment of foreign currency loans. Banks' funding positions remained broadly sound. The HKD loan-to-deposit ratio fell slightly to 77.1% at the end of 2016, reflecting that deposit growth outpaced loan growth. The overall foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio dropped to 59.9% at the end of the year, and the USD loan-to-deposit ratio fell significantly to 63.8% due to strong growth in USD deposits. Due to the strong US dollar, both onshore and offshore RMB exchange rates weakened. Against this backdrop, Hong Kong's offshore RMB liquidity pool (comprising customer deposits and outstanding certificates of deposit) consolidated further along with other offshore RMB markets, and the volatility of offshore RMB HIBORs increased significantly. Nevertheless, banks' RMB liquidity management remained robust, and the average daily turnover of the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement system stayed at a high level. Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is likely to continue facing headwinds brought about by uncertainties in the RMB exchange rate movements. With improving global market conditions, the Hong Kong stock market closed significantly higher during the reporting period. Although the US presidential election yielded an unexpected outcome, the market experienced only a brief shock. This was mainly because investors' hopes for fiscal stimulus measures by the Trump administration drove global stock markets higher. While benefiting from this, the local market also exhibited caution amidst the optimism, likely due to concerns over a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, challenges facing the Mainland's economic outlook, uncertainties in RMB policy, and controls on capital flows. Looking ahead, although the local market may be affected by external economic conditions, its attractive valuation could provide support to the market. Although HKD bond yields rose sharply late last year and their yield spreads against US Treasury bonds widened rapidly, the HKD bond market continued to expand steadily during the reporting period. Meanwhile, Hong Kong's offshore RMB bond market recovered in the second half of 2016 after contracting in the first half, but new bond issuance recorded for the full year still decreased compared to the previous year. Looking ahead, if global investors reverse their earlier search-for-yield investment strategies, both the HKD and offshore RMB bond markets will come under pressure. As US trade policies remain unclear and the RMB exchange rate may remain volatile, the outlook for these two bond markets over the next six months will continue to be clouded by significant uncertainties. Following the introduction of the new stamp duty measure by the Government, the residential property market showed signs of adjustment immediately, but has rebounded recently. In view of renewed market exuberance, the Government raised the stamp duty to a flat rate of 15% in November. Transaction volumes in both the primary and secondary markets fell in the subsequent two months. However, transaction volumes have risen recently, partly reflecting developers' increased launches of primary market projects. At the same time, property prices continued to rise to new highs, although the upward momentum has moderated.

Following the unexpected election of Donald Trump as US President, uncertainty surrounding US policy has increased. Although market focus is concentrated on the short-term benefits of potential large-scale fiscal policies and pro-business measures, US economic activity is currently close to its economic potential. Fiscal stimulus measures may only provide a mild cyclical boost to US economic growth, but will further exacerbate the upside risks to inflation. More importantly, the risks faced by emerging market economies are increasing along with the capital outflow pressure brought by the accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes and a stronger US dollar, while potential trade protectionist measures by the US will also threaten global trade flows. In East Asia, real economic activity improved slightly in the second half of 2016, and recent export volumes have also increased. However, against the backdrop of US interest rate hikes, US dollar appreciation, and potential US protectionist measures, financial markets are expected to remain volatile, and downside risks to economic growth are rising. In Mainland China, overall economic growth accelerated slightly in the second half of 2016 amid solid growth in infrastructure investment and improved business spending in the private sector. The Mainland economy continues to rebalance, with the tertiary sector expanding steadily, but the ongoing advancement of economic structural adjustments and changes in Sino-US trade relations may increase uncertainty in the short-term economic outlook. With the government determined to curb rising housing prices, if the property market continues to cool, the real estate sector's contribution to economic growth this year may also decrease. On the external front, although the RMB remained stable against the China Foreign Exchange Trade System (CFETS) basket of currencies during the reporting period, capital outflow pressure increased at the end of 2016 amid US dollar appreciation and US interest rate hikes, and subsequently appeared to ease slightly in early 2017. Following the unexpected election of Donald Trump as US President, global financial markets reacted strongly, particularly as market expectations that Trump's policies of tax reform, large-scale increases in infrastructure spending, and deregulation would push up US economic growth and inflation, stimulating a rally in major stock markets (Chart 2.1). Consequently, market expectations for US inflation and US interest rate hikes heated up, causing US Treasury yields to surge and the US dollar to strengthen. Chart 2.1 Stock Market Indices of Selected Advanced Economies However, the Trump tax cuts anticipated by the market may fail to generate the positive impact on US economic growth expected by the market. Although a shift in economic policy towards reliance on fiscal easing measures would help alleviate the heavy burden borne by monetary easing policies, given the current stage of the US economic cycle, whether now is the appropriate time to implement fiscal easing measures is debatable. Although the pace of US economic growth has slowed in recent quarters, the output gap is gradually narrowing, and the February unemployment rate also matched the Federal Reserve's estimated natural rate of unemployment of 4.7%, reflecting that US economic activity is already close to its economic potential. The US economy is currently in an expansionary cycle, and the fiscal multiplier will be lower than during a recession (for example, see Auerbach and Gorodnichenko (2012)) 1. In fact, recent estimates of the US Laffer curve indicate that tax cuts on labor or capital could lead to a reduction in tax revenue (for example, see Trabandt and Uhlig (2012)) 2. In any case, with diminishing excess capacity, any further measures to boost economic growth, even if their real impact on economic growth is limited, could push up inflation. Meanwhile, other factors such as rising oil and commodity prices, as well as potential trade protectionist measures including the Border Adjustment Tax currently under consideration, could also exacerbate the upside risks to US inflation. Even with the increased risk of rising US inflation, the Federal Reserve remains cautious about tightening US monetary policy and tends to maintain an ultra-loose monetary policy stance. However, long-term bond yields have already risen, partly reflecting the increased risk of US inflation. Since the US election, although market forecasts for the future federal funds rate have been revised upwards to near the median of the Federal Reserve's projections for 2017 and early 2018, they remain well below the Federal Reserve's longer-run projections (Chart 2.2). Therefore, an accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes could trigger the risk of significant market volatility. Although financial markets are focused on the short-term benefits of stronger US economic growth driven by potentially implemented expansionary fiscal policies and pro-business measures, long-term risks remain, including damaging protectionist trade policies and a further rise in US national debt. In fact, the Trump administration may fulfill its campaign promises by adopting trade protectionist measures. Increased trade barriers would lead to market distortions that harm overall interests, hinder global trade flows, reduce the efficiency of global supply chains, and pose downside risks to the global economic outlook. Chart 2.2 Future Federal Funds Rate Projections: Federal Reserve vs. Market In Europe, political instability remains a major risk and headwind to the European economic recovery. Although the economic environment in the Eurozone is gradually improving, with real GDP in the fourth quarter growing moderately by 1.7% year-on-year, only slightly lower than the 1.8% year-on-year increase in the third quarter, compared to the stronger recovery of the US economy, economic activity in the Eurozone is still only slightly above pre-global financial crisis levels (Chart 2.3). Since the Brexit decision last summer, the market has been concerned about the eventual breakup of the Eurozone. Although Italy's economic and political situation appears to have stabilized following the formation of a new government and the implementation of banking sector rescue measures, against the backdrop of Brexit negotiations and rising anti-establishment sentiment, upcoming elections in Germany and France (and possibly Italy) could become political flashpoints. Partly due to increased political uncertainty, European sovereign bond yields have continued to climb, and corporate bond spreads have also widened. This situation is particularly evident in peripheral countries, potentially creating a vicious cycle for the real economy and putting pressure on real business investment in the Eurozone. Chart 2.3 Real GDP of Major Advanced Economies In Japan, real GDP in recent quarters has been revised upwards, with the annualized growth rate in the fourth quarter of 2016 increasing to 1.6% year-on-year, the fastest pace since the third quarter of 2015, indicating a stronger economic recovery than previously expected. However, partly due to structural issues in the labor market, wage growth has been slow, leading to weak consumption growth. Meanwhile, the recent rapid depreciation of the Japanese yen means that the downward pressure on "new core" goods inflation caused by the earlier appreciation of the yen is about to start fading. Coupled with a stronger-than-expected recovery, this indicates an improvement in the short-term inflation outlook, and although "new core" inflation (excluding fresh food and energy) fell to 0.1% in December, it is expected to bottom out and rebound. Nevertheless, facing long-term and structural headwinds, growth is likely to remain sluggish, and inflation expectations remain at around 0.5% – 0.6%, lower than the levels when Abenomics was introduced in early 2014. Therefore, the risk that the inflation rate will fail to meet the Bank of Japan's medium-term target of 2% still exists. For other countries, especially emerging market economies, the benefits of faster US economic growth transmitted through trade channels may be smaller due to reduced US imports following the global financial crisis and the possibility of the US implementing protectionist policies. At the same time, the accelerated pace of US interest rate hikes and further appreciation of the US dollar will lead to a tightening of financial conditions, exacerbating downside economic risks. This could drag down economic growth and increase the risk of rapid capital outflows. In fact, market expectations of large-scale fiscal expansion by the Trump administration, coupled with concerns over surging energy prices, have led to a repricing of inflation risks, resulting in a broad and significant rise in long-term bond yields across advanced economies and many emerging market economies. Feature 1 assesses the potential spillover effects of US interest rate hike expectations on the sovereign bond markets of 26 selected economies. In East Asia 3, real economic activity has recently regained momentum, with regional GDP growing modestly and inflation rising. Real GDP Growth — In the second half of 2016, economic growth generally remained stable due to steady private consumption in several regional economies. Meanwhile, exports generally recorded a modest increase from their 2015 lows. This benefited not only from the stabilization of China's growth but also from the improved performance of advanced economies such as the US and Europe. For net commodity exporters (such as Malaysia and Indonesia), the rebound in commodity prices also provided an additional boost. Other major exporters (such as South Korea, Taiwan, and Singapore) also regained upward momentum due to growth in electronics and semiconductor exports. Inflation — With the rebound in commodity (especially oil) prices, producer price inflation has generally shown an upward trend. Although this will push up industrial costs or even consumer spending, consumption and investment growth may increase due to the decline in long-term deflation risks. Accelerated producer price inflation may exert upward pressure on consumer price inflation, with the actual impact depending on the extent to which the increase in producer prices is passed on to consumer prices, which varies across economies. Consensus forecasts for the Consumer Price Index indicate that although inflation in several regional economies will still be slightly below their respective central banks' 2017 inflation targets, it will rise closer to the target levels (Chart 2.4). With the exception of Indonesia, central banks in the East Asian region have generally maintained their accommodative monetary policies with unchanged interest rates; Indonesia cut interest rates twice in September and October last year to boost growth. Chart 2.4 Headline CPI Inflation, Forecasts, and Central Bank Targets in the East Asian Region Despite the improvement in the real economy, the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election in November 2016 triggered short-term volatility in financial markets. Foreign Exchange Markets — Following the US presidential election, investors expected US inflation to rise, and most regional currencies depreciated against the US dollar. However, on a trade-weighted basis, some regional currencies have depreciated to a lesser extent or even appreciated slightly since the US election (Chart 2.5). Chart 2.5 Spot FX Depreciation against the US Dollar and Changes in Nominal Effective Exchange Rates Post-US Election Bond and Stock Markets — Asset prices briefly plunged following the US presidential election but quickly stabilized. The spreads between sovereign bonds of East Asian economies and US Treasury bonds widened. However, as markets stabilized, yields in some regional economies declined, although they have not yet returned to pre-election levels (Chart 2.6). Nevertheless, spreads have narrowed compared to pre-election levels. Chart 2.6 Spreads between 10-Year Sovereign Bonds and US Treasury Bonds Portfolio Investment Flows — Portfolio investment funds flowed out of the East Asian region in the fourth quarter of 2016, but at a slower pace than during the "taper tantrum" in mid-2013. By the first few weeks of 2017, capital inflows were recorded again, supporting asset prices and financial conditions. Looking ahead, growth in the region is expected to remain stable, but the pace will still be lower than the historical average. Due to rising uncertainty regarding US government policies and the potential policy responses from the Federal Reserve, financial markets are highly likely to remain volatile. A significant rise in the US dollar and yields could attract capital flows from the region to the US, prompting investors to reduce their holdings of regional assets, which is particularly concerning for assets with currently high valuations. A tightening of financial conditions under such circumstances would also put repayment pressure on enterprises with large amounts of US dollar-denominated debt. Macroeconomically, a general global interest rate hike would also reduce fixed capital investment in the region, which would not only drag down aggregate demand in the short term but could also affect potential growth in the long term. Finally, exporting countries in the region face the potential threat of trade protectionist policies implemented by the new US administration. The US trade deficit with East Asian economies has continued to widen in recent years (Chart 2.7), especially in the region's major export industries, such as electronics, electrical appliances, automobiles, apparel, and textiles. Over the past two decades, increased US imports in these industries have led to massive job losses. Protectionist policies aimed at reducing the trade deficit and revitalizing US manufacturing could pose significant risks to exporting countries in the region.

Accelerated growth in private consumption and robust building and construction activities in the public sector drove a slight pickup in Hong Kong's economic growth in the second half of 2016. Due to an increasingly uncertain external environment, economic growth is expected to be moderate in 2017. Benefiting from stable import prices and moderate domestic growth momentum, inflation pressures are expected to remain contained. Hong Kong's economic growth picked up slightly in the second half of 2016. Seasonally adjusted real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew by 1.2% quarter-on-quarter in Q4, slightly higher than the 0.8% growth rate in Q3 (Chart 3.1). Partly due to improved consumer sentiment and stable labour market conditions, the growth of private consumption accelerated, becoming the main driver of GDP growth. Supported by infrastructure projects such as the third runway at the Hong Kong International Airport, building and construction activities also became robust. However, due to weak corporate capital expenditure, the contribution of overall investment spending to GDP growth narrowed. On the external front, both exports and imports of goods accelerated in tandem with rising regional trade flows (Chart 3.2). 22 Trade-related and transportation services drove further growth in exports of services, while imports of services rebounded partly due to strong travel demand from local residents. Net exports continued to drag on GDP growth.  Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real exports and imports The labour market remained tight. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate held steady at 3.4% in the first three quarters, before edging down to 3.3% in Q4 (Chart 3.3). In fact, the unemployment rates in several major sectors declined during the second half of the year, including the retail, accommodation and food services sectors, partly because the slowdown in the retail sector had somewhat stabilized. Total employment reached a new high of 3.824 million in February 2017, while the labour force participation rate remained stable at around 61%.  Chart 3.3 Unemployment rate and total employment Real economic growth is expected to remain moderate in 2017. On the external front, global economic and trade growth may remain moderate due to the uncertain global macroeconomic and financial environment. Coupled with the strong US dollar leading to an increase in the real effective exchange rate of the Hong Kong dollar, this will constrain Hong Kong's export performance. On the domestic front, although stable employment and income conditions will support consumption, private consumption is expected to grow moderately, dragged down by rising interest rates. With the increase in housing supply and the rollout of various infrastructure projects, building and construction activities should grow steadily, but subdued business sentiment and rising interest rates will dampen corporate capital expenditure. The Government currently forecasts real GDP growth for 2017 to be between 2% and 3%, while the average forecast by private sector analysts is 2.0%. The economic growth outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties, particularly those stemming from the external environment. Policy uncertainties of the new US administration will cloud the global economic outlook, and potential trade protectionist policies could pose headwinds to global trade flows. The Brexit process and general elections in several major European countries may also lead to asset market volatility and affect Hong Kong dollar fund flows. Furthermore, US interest rate normalization will tighten domestic monetary conditions and exert downward pressure on the real economy and asset prices.  Since the second half of 2016, although domestic inflation has seen an increase in quarter-on-quarter momentum in recent months, it has remained moderate overall. On a year-on-year basis, the underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (Composite CPI) remained stable at 2.1% from the second half of 2016 to January this year (Chart 3.4). The underlying inflation rate on an annualized 3-month basis, which reflects inflation momentum, accelerated from 0.9% in Q3 to 3.0% in Q4, before easing slightly to 2.4% in January. The rise in inflation momentum was mainly driven by higher prices of tradables and housing rentals (Chart 3.5). In particular, tradables price inflation rose from a negative figure in Q3 to 3.0% in Q4, mainly driven by the prices of basic foodstuffs and clothing and footwear. Meanwhile, since Q3, with the narrowing decline in private housing rentals and the upward adjustment of public housing rentals in September 2016, the housing rental component of the Composite CPI increased, but subsequently moderated slightly in January (Chart 3.6).  Chart 3.4 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Consumer price inflation by major component Chart 3.6 Composite CPI rental component and market rentals In the near term, inflation pressures are expected to remain contained due to weak import prices and moderate domestic cost pressures. As the strong Hong Kong dollar partially offsets the impact of the rebound in global commodity prices, imported inflation will remain low (Chart 3.7). Domestically, the output gap was estimated to remain close to zero in Q4 2016, which should help alleviate business cost pressures and thereby restrain inflation in the services components. Despite the tight labour market, wage increases have been mild in recent quarters; real payroll per person engaged rose by 1.1% in the first half of 2016, before falling by 0.4% in Q3 (Chart 3.8). Given the persistently uncertain external environment leading to cautious business sentiment, the increase in labour costs should be restrained against this backdrop. In addition, due to the sluggish retail sales performance in recent months, the increase in retail property rentals is expected to be moderate. Furthermore, the impact of the earlier softening in private housing rentals will gradually surface, which will also help ease inflation pressures. Overall, the year-on-year inflation rate for the whole of 2017 is expected to decline; the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate for the year to be 2.0%, lower than the 2.3% in 2016.  Chart 3.7 Commodity and import prices Chart 3.8 Unit labour cost and real payroll per person engaged The inflation outlook faces both upside and downside risks. On the downside risks, if inflation accelerates under the Trump administration in the US, it could lead to a faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes, which may push up domestic mortgage rates and increase downward pressure on property prices and housing rentals. At the same time, the appreciation of the Hong Kong dollar may keep import prices weak and simultaneously weaken the city's attractiveness to inbound tourists. On the upside risks, if the global economic expansion is faster than expected, it may accelerate Hong Kong's economic growth and push up demand-driven international commodity prices, thereby exerting upward pressure on domestic inflation. In addition, the upwardly adjusted Statutory Minimum Wage will take effect on May 1, 2017, which may cause inflation to rise further, but the actual impact of this cost-push inflation will depend on the extent to which wage costs are passed on to consumer prices.

Despite financial market volatility, the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate remained broadly stable, while the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) rose in tandem with US dollar (USD) interbank rates. Overall loans continued to grow moderately, partly due to an improved domestic economic environment. Looking ahead, the volatility of HKD fund flows may increase amid a faster pace of US interest rate normalization, the uncertain policy direction of the new US administration, and political risks in Europe. Despite financial market volatility, the spot exchange rate of the HKD against the USD remained broadly stable (Chart 4.1). Although market volatility triggered by the US presidential election in November caused Asian currencies to fall generally, the HKD spot exchange rate against the USD remained steady. However, the interest rate projections announced by the US Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) at its meeting on December 13-14, 2016, fueled market expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, causing the HKD to weaken briefly thereafter. In early 2017, the HKD exchange rate strengthened somewhat along with other Asian currencies, but as market expectations for a US rate hike in March rose from mid-February, the HKD began to show signs of weakening. During the reporting period, the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 Exchange rate and fund flow indicators Chart 4.2 Fund flow indicators Along with the strong USD, the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) index of the HKD rose by 4.9% between August and December, before stabilizing recently (Chart 4.3). As the impact of the narrowing inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was mild, the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) index of the HKD closely tracked the movements of the NEER index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and real effective exchange rates Portfolio investment recorded outflows in the second half of 2016. The latest Balance of Payments statistics showed net inflows of non-resident equity and debt securities investments in the third quarter, reflecting improved global market sentiment and abundant Initial Public Offering (IPO) activities (Table 4.A). However, driven partly by Hong Kong banks increasing their holdings of US bonds, residents' debt investments recorded massive outflows, which more than offset the investment inflows from non-residents. Consequently, cross-border portfolio investment recorded a net outflow in the third quarter. A survey of global mutual funds indicated portfolio investment outflows in the last quarter of 2016, mainly due to the unexpected outcome of the US presidential election and expectations of a faster pace of US interest rate hikes, which put pressure on the local financial market and other Asian markets (Chart 4.4). However, the latest data showed that Hong Kong portfolio investment experienced capital inflow pressures in the first quarter of 2017, partly due to investors' optimism about the US adopting expansionary fiscal policies, which improved the performance of global financial markets. Chart 4.4 Market survey of equity and bond-related fund flows Looking ahead, the volatility of HKD fund flows may increase. A faster pace of US interest rate normalization would increase the risk of a reversal in HKD fund flows. At the same time, fund flows may become more volatile amid uncertainties surrounding the new US administration, the Brexit process, and elections in European Union member states. In addition, increased investment demand for HKD assets from Mainland investors may exert capital inflow pressures on the HKD. Although the scale of Northbound trading exceeded that of Southbound trading in the initial period following the launch of the Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect in December, two-way equity investment fund flows between the Mainland and Hong Kong under the scheme are expected to increase gradually. Despite rising USD interest rates and financial market volatility, Hong Kong's monetary conditions remained accommodative in the second half of 2016 and in recent months. The HKD monetary base remained massive, rising further by 1.7% in the second half of the year, driven by the growth in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation (Chart 4.5). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered, the sum of the Aggregate Balance and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) remained broadly stable at a high level of HK$1,222.7 billion. Within this total, due to the additional issuance of HK$49 billion of Exchange Fund Bills to meet banks' strong demand for liquidity management, the Aggregate Balance contracted while outstanding EFBNs increased correspondingly. Chart 4.5 Components of the monetary base As the domestic economy gradually firmed up, the pace of HKD money supply growth accelerated. The growth of HKD broad money supply (HKD M3) picked up from 2.3% in the first half of the year to 6.5% in the second half. As a major component of HKD M3, HKD deposits recorded a faster growth of 6.6% in the second half of the year (Chart 4.7), mainly driven by stronger domestic economic activities and increased transaction demand stemming from a rebound in IPO activities. Analyzed by counterpart assets, the growth of HKD M3 mainly reflected increases in HKD loans and banks' net foreign currency assets (Chart 4.6), which represented money created from credit expansion and net HKD fund inflows from the non-bank private sector, respectively. Chart 4.6 Changes in HKD M3 and its counterpart assets On the other hand, the growth of foreign currency deposits remained mixed. After growing by 10.2% in the first half of the year, USD deposits recorded a higher increase of 12.8% in the second half amid the strong USD (Chart 4.7). In contrast, other foreign currency deposits contracted further by 10.3%, mainly due to a decline in Renminbi (RMB) deposits. Overall, total deposits with Authorized Institutions grew at an accelerated pace of 6.2% in the second half of 2016, and by 9.1% for the whole year. Driven by stronger domestic economic activities and increased cross-border funding demand, overall loans rose further by 4.2% in the second half of the year, following a 2.2% growth in the first half (Chart 4.10). Loans for use outside Hong Kong rebounded by 4.6% in the second half after a slight decline in the first half, partly reflecting increased year-end funding demand from multinational corporations. Analyzed by currency, HKD loans grew strongly by 5.0% in the second half, and foreign currency loans also recorded a moderate growth of 3.2% as Mainland borrowers gradually reduced their repayment of foreign currency loans. Due to the appreciation of the USD, both offshore and onshore Renminbi (RMB) exchange rates weakened (Chart 4.14). The offshore RMB exchange rate traded at a discount to the onshore RMB exchange rate for most of the latter part of 2016, closing at an intra-year low of 6.98 against the USD at the end of 2016. The offshore RMB interbank market experienced renewed liquidity tightening pressure in December, partly reflecting deteriorating financial market conditions and banks' precautionary funding demand ahead of the year-end (Chart 4.15). As banks increased their liquidity buffers amid worsening market sentiment, the overnight CNH Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (CNH HIBOR) surged to 61.3% at one point on January 6, 2017. The rise in offshore RMB funding costs subsequently led to the unwinding of short offshore RMB positions, driving a rebound in the offshore RMB exchange rate in early January 2017, and the spread between the offshore and onshore RMB also turned into a premium. Since mid-January, the offshore and onshore RMB exchange rates have stabilized somewhat, and liquidity conditions have gradually improved, with the overnight and 3-month CNH HIBOR falling to 2.00% and 4.61% respectively at the end of February 2017.

In the second half of 2016, the profitability of retail banks improved compared to the same period in 2015, driven by the growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as a reduction in loan impairment provisions. The capital positions and asset quality of banks also remained sound. Although the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) rose significantly following the US interest rate hike in December, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained sound. The funding costs of retail banks remained stable and at low levels, supported by a massive retail deposit base. However, banks should carefully assess the impact of a potentially faster-than-expected pace of US interest rate hikes, particularly the risk of massive capital outflows and their subsequent potential impact on local interest rates. Furthermore, given the continuous rise in the leverage levels of non-local corporates, a sharp increase in interest rates could lead to a deterioration in banks' asset quality. To enhance the resilience of Hong Kong banks against systemic risks, the countercyclical capital buffer ratio requirement will be increased to 1.875% effective from 1 January 2018.   The profitability of retail banks improved, with the return on assets rising from 0.95% in the second half of 2015 to 1.12% in the second half of 2016 (red line in Chart 5.1). The factors contributing to the profitability improvement were the growth in net interest income and non-interest income, as well as the reduction in loan impairment provisions. For the full year of 2016, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks grew by 8.7%, while the return on assets rose from 1.05% for the full year of 2015 to 1.10%. In the longer term, as the US will further raise interest rates, banks may soon face upward pressure on retail deposit rates, thereby affecting their funding costs and exerting a more significant impact on net interest margins.
