On a half-yearly basis, the growth of personal loans slowed from 5.3% in the first half of 2018 to 3.9% in the second half. This was mainly due to a slowdown in the growth of private purpose loans (including credit card advances and other loans for private purposes), which offset the rapid growth of residential mortgage loans (Table 5.B). As Hong Kong's nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) grew at a slower pace than personal loans, the household debt-to-GDP ratio edged up from 71.2% in the second quarter of 2018 to 71.9% in the fourth quarter (Chart 5.14).

The coronavirus outbreak, which erupted in early 2020, has hit both demand and supply, posing challenges to the global economy that are distinct from previous crises. Although major central banks and some governments have rolled out stimulus measures since early March to stem the economic impact brought by the pandemic, financial markets remain volatile, and global financial conditions have also tightened. Despite uncertainties in the external and domestic environments, the Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. With a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable Aggregate Balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no noticeable fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. After a mild rebound in the first half of 2019, total loan growth slowed down in the second half of the year. The residential property market has generally softened since mid-2019, though its trajectory has been somewhat volatile. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continuous rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, global economic growth has shown initial signs of stabilization, benefiting from increased monetary easing by major central banks, the easing of US-China trade tensions, and the receding risk of a "no-deal Brexit" for the UK. However, since late January, the continuous increase in global coronavirus infection cases has raised market concerns and triggered significant volatility in global financial markets. To address the evolving risks of the pandemic, several major central banks have substantially cut interest rates and expanded liquidity tools, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support the real economy. Nevertheless, amid widening credit spreads and plunging stock markets, global financial conditions have tightened. Looking ahead, downside risks to the global economic outlook have increased. The coronavirus pandemic will hit global economic activities, and the extent of the economic impact will depend on the severity and duration of the pandemic. In the medium term, relations between the US and its major trading partners may become tense again, and post-Brexit trade negotiations between the UK and the EU may also be fraught with difficulties. Weak global demand continues to drag down economic growth in the East Asian region1. Exports from the East Asian region to major destinations such as the US, European economies, and Mainland China remained weak in the second half of 2019. Some major telecommunications equipment exporters in the region have recently reported revenue growth, but whether the tech product cycle will rebound broadly remains to be seen. Financial markets reacted positively to the US-China phase one trade deal announced in December 2019, and the trade truce has to some extent reduced uncertainties in global trade. Nonetheless, the East Asian region will continue to face headwinds such as weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage ratios. At the same time, the coronavirus outbreak has sparked concerns that the regional economy may come under further pressure amid persistently weak growth. Travel bans implemented by various economies in the region may hit Asia's tourism industry, especially those economies that rely more heavily on tourism service exports. Given the close supply chain linkages between the region and Mainland China, the manufacturing sector may also be affected by the outbreak. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the US-China phase one trade deal helps temporarily reduce external uncertainties facing the Mainland economy, downward pressure remains amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and the global economic slowdown. The Central Economic Work Conference held in December 2019 set economic stability as the priority for 2020, while also focusing on the control of financial risks. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that Mainland economic growth will slow to 5.2% in 2020. During the review period, Mainland authorities continued to announce targeted monetary and fiscal policies to support the private sector, particularly small private enterprises. Despite these measures, some media reports and market analysts have pointed out that private industrial enterprises may have faced a decline in shareholders' equity in recent years, which is seen as a sign of a "retreat of the private sector". Box 2 examines the drivers of equity changes in Mainland industrial enterprises using 2018 listed company data, and finds that private or small enterprises are not inherently more vulnerable to downsizing or "retreat". Although the study finds that negative profitability is the biggest driver, other factors, especially structural ones, are also noteworthy (see Box 2 for details). Hong Kong's economic activities contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) declined continuously over the past three quarters, indicating that the Hong Kong economy has entered a recession. Dragged down by this, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the whole of 2019, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, and marking the first annual contraction since 2009. The slowdown in domestic demand, particularly the contraction in private consumption, was the main factor dragging down GDP in the second half of 2019. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities, leading to a weak economic outlook and thereby dampening consumer and business confidence. With the re-escalation of US-China trade frictions, the slowdown in global economic growth, and a severe setback in inbound tourism, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish. Given the significant headwinds facing the economy, the Government rolled out multiple rounds of economic stimulus measures between August and December 2019. To allow banks more headroom to step up their support for the domestic economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on October 14 a reduction of the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion of lending capacity to enterprises, especially small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the pandemic has recently also brought notable downside risks. As sectors such as retail, accommodation services, food and beverage services, tourism, and transport have yet to recover from the disruptions caused by the social incidents, the pandemic will deal a double blow to these sectors. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020/21 Budget can provide relief to households and enterprises (especially SMEs), including a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and the provision of a concessionary low-interest loan with a 100% government guarantee for enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme.2 The HKMA further reduced the CCyB ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on March 16, 2020, which will allow banks more headroom to step up their support for the domestic economy, especially for sectors and individuals facing greater pressure in the near term due to the impact of the pandemic. Analyzed by GDP components, private consumption and investment are likely to remain weak due to fragile consumer and business confidence. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the US-China phase one trade deal is expected to have a mild positive impact on the domestic economy in the near term.3 However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to drag down Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to supply chain disruptions in the region and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 to range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is subject to numerous uncertainties and risks, including the global economic slowdown, US-China trade relations, Mainland China's economic performance, and local social incidents. The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020, with total employment decreasing, the unemployment rate rising, and the real payroll index falling year-on-year. Specifically, the unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.7% in February 2020, partly reflecting the impact of the social incidents and the pandemic outbreak on the retail, accommodation, and food and beverage services sectors. Looking ahead, given the weak economic outlook and the coronavirus outbreak, the unemployment rate is expected to climb further. Box 3 will discuss the recent developments and near-term outlook of the labor market in greater detail. Domestic inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly driven by the surge in fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activities weakened, inflation momentum also gradually slowed. Due to weak economic conditions, the consolidation of private residential rentals, and mild imported inflation, inflation is expected to ease in the near term. Market consensus forecasts headline inflation for 2020 to range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts an underlying inflation rate of 2.5%. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the Hong Kong dollar (including Initial Public Offerings (IPOs)), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October 2019. Entering December, the upward momentum of the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate strengthened further, partly due to robust IPO activities, and partly due to the unwinding of short Hong Kong dollar positions prompted by tighter liquidity towards the year-end. After the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity conditions eased somewhat, and the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened slightly towards the end of February. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period, and the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered. The Aggregate Balance remained stable at around HK$54 billion. Since the fourth quarter of 2019, short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) have exhibited volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities such as IPOs. Box 4 examines how market attention to future IPO activities affects the 3-month HIBOR. Meanwhile, the Composite Interest Rate gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020, reflecting that banks continued to raise promotional deposit rates to attract deposit funds. As some banks raised the interest rate caps priced against the Prime Rate, the average interest rate for newly approved mortgage loans rose to around 2.6% in October, but as the Prime Rates in the market were lowered from November onwards, the average interest rate for newly approved mortgage loans fell slightly to around 2.5% by January 2020. With a stronger Hong Kong dollar exchange rate, a stable Aggregate Balance, and moderate growth in total deposits, no noticeable fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system were observed during the review period. However, we need to monitor the impact of any further deterioration of the coronavirus pandemic amid an uncertain external environment. Hong Kong has massive foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system; the HKMA has the capability, resources, and resolve to cope with fund outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. During the review period, driven by market expectations of a US-China trade deal, the offshore and onshore Renminbi exchange rates strengthened, but have faced weakening pressure since late January 2020 due to the coronavirus outbreak. In the latter part of 2019, the offshore Renminbi generally traded at a premium to the onshore Renminbi; the discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, but the spread remained modest by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore Renminbi liquidity pool rebounded slightly after a mild decline in the previous review period. As of the end of January 2020, outstanding Renminbi customer deposits and certificates of deposit increased to RMB 637.4 billion. Hong Kong's other Renminbi businesses also grew, with Renminbi bank lending and Renminbi trade settlement businesses in Hong Kong recording strong growth. The daily average turnover of the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system remained at a high level of RMB 1,133.9 billion for the whole of 2019. Despite uncertainties in the external environment, Hong Kong's offshore Renminbi business is expected to benefit from the continuous opening up of the Mainland's capital account, increased allocation to Renminbi assets by international investors, and deepening regional economic and financial cooperation under the "Belt and Road" and "Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area" initiatives.

At the end of 2019, global economic activity showed signs of stabilization, raising market expectations for a global economic recovery. However, since late January 2020, the continuous increase in global coronavirus infection cases has dashed these recovery expectations, deepening investors' concerns about a global economic recession and triggering a sell-off in global financial markets. To cope with the economic shock, major central banks and some governments have introduced stimulus measures since early March. Given the spread of the epidemic, downside risks to the global economic growth outlook have increased. In East Asia, weak global demand since the second half of 2019 has cast a shadow over the outlook for economies in the region. The coronavirus outbreak is expected to drag down regional economic growth in the short term, with the tourism sector being hit particularly hard. On the other hand, the East Asian region also continues to face the challenges of weak corporate earnings and high private sector leverage ratios. As for Mainland China, economic growth continued to slow down in the second half of 2019 due to weak domestic and external demand. Looking ahead, although the signing of the phase one trade agreement between China and the US helps temporarily reduce external uncertainties, downside pressures remain amid the coronavirus outbreak, ongoing economic rebalancing, and the global economic slowdown, while the authorities' monetary and fiscal policy responses will provide some buffer. Under the impact of persistent trade tensions and policy uncertainties, manufacturing and investment remained weak, and global economic growth remained sluggish in the second half of 2019. However, economic growth showed preliminary signs of stabilization in the final quarter (Chart 2.1), partly benefiting from the earlier easing policies of the US Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank, as well as the easing of global trade tensions following the signing of the "phase one" trade agreement between China and the US. Chart 2.1 Manufacturing Purchasing Managers' Index However, since late January, the continuous increase in global coronavirus infection cases and the subsequent economic shocks have raised market concerns, leading to a wave of sell-offs in global financial markets (Chart 2.2). Given that Mainland China is a major global export destination and plays an important role in global supply chains, when the epidemic disrupts its domestic production activities and drags down its economic growth, it will cause significant spillover effects and potentially affect the globe (Chart 2.3). Since late February, the surge in coronavirus infection cases outside Mainland China may exacerbate supply chain disruptions and pose a risk of directly dragging down local economic activities. 5 Chart 2.2 MSCI All Country World Index and Bloomberg Barclays Global Corporate Bond Index Option-Adjusted Spread Chart 2.3 Goods and Services Exports to Mainland China by Selected Major Advanced Economies in 2018 (% of GDP) To cope with the potential severe economic shocks caused by the epidemic, some central banks (including the US Federal Reserve, the Bank of Canada, and the Bank of England) have cut interest rates since early March, while some governments have also introduced targeted measures to support households and businesses. However, financial markets still face immense selling pressure, leading to a significant tightening of global financial conditions, which in turn may exacerbate downside pressures on the global economy (Chart 2.4). Chart 2.4 Bloomberg Advanced Economies Financial Conditions Index Apart from the development of the epidemic, other downside risks and uncertainties also cloud the global economic outlook. Particularly regarding trade tensions, although policy risks have decreased following the phase one trade agreement between China and the US, subsequent negotiations may be fraught with difficulties as many thorny structural issues remain to be resolved. In Europe, trade negotiations between the EU and the UK are not expected to be smooth, thereby prolonging post-Brexit uncertainties. In addition, the sharp drop in oil prices since March will exert pressure on major oil-exporting emerging economies. In East Asia, real economic activity remained sluggish in the second half of 2019 due to subdued global demand. Exports from the East Asian region to various major destinations, such as the US, European economies, and Mainland China, remained weak in the second half of 2019 (Chart 2.5). Although there are preliminary signs that the downcycle of technology products in the region is bottoming out, including reports from large regional electronics companies that their earnings improved at the end of 2019, 6 it remains to be seen whether there will be a substantial rebound in the region's technology product exports. Chart 2.5 East Asia: Merchandise Exports to Major Destinations Persistently weak economic growth and trade uncertainties have also troubled investor sentiment, with gross fixed capital formation in most East Asian economies declining in 2019 (Chart 2.6), which may affect the region's potential economic growth in the long run. To support economic growth in a mild inflation environment, the central banks of Indonesia, the Philippines, and South Korea lowered their policy rates again in the second half of 2019 after cutting rates in the first half, while the Bank of Thailand also lowered its policy rate for the first time since 2015. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Gross Fixed Capital Formation The coronavirus outbreak has led to concerns that economies in the region may face further pressure amid persistently weak growth. As multiple economies in the region have imposed travel restrictions on Mainland China, the tourism sector has borne the brunt, with economies more reliant on Mainland Chinese tourists and tourism service exports being more severely affected by this epidemic (Chart 2.7). The continuation and intensification of the epidemic will also affect supply chains in the region that are closely linked to Mainland China. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Tourism Exports and Chinese Tourists In the short term, this epidemic will continue to affect economic activities and investor sentiment. Drawing on the experience of the 2003 SARS outbreak, these impacts may be short-lived, but the actual situation will depend on the severity of the epidemic, the extent of its spread, and the effectiveness of government actions to contain the outbreak. At the same time, East Asian economies also face multiple headwinds. First, although the market expects corporate earnings to deteriorate in the short term (Chart 2.8), accommodative global monetary conditions encourage search-for-yield activities, thereby pushing up asset prices without fundamental support. Therefore, regional stock markets are more vulnerable to shifts in investor sentiment. Chart 2.8 Expected Earnings of Benchmark Stock Index Constituents Second, weak corporate earnings and economic growth may make it more difficult for private sector entities in the region to service their debts. Although lower domestic interest rates can provide breathing space for indebted companies and households, they may also sow the seeds for further debt accumulation. Furthermore, as discussed in Box 1, when more index-tracking funds flow into regional financial markets, the risk of debt overhang in the private sector may also intensify, although this impact may be limited to enterprises with sounder financial fundamentals and their long-term borrowings. Third, regarding external factors, East Asian economies may face increased risks in the face of US trade policies with increasingly tough protectionist barriers. Despite recent progress on the phase one trade agreement between China and the US, Sino-US trade tensions persist as fundamental trade issues between the two countries remain. As evidenced by the widening trade surpluses of multiple regional economies with the US (Chart 2.9), multinational companies may continue to seek more sourcing channels outside the China-centric supply chains to circumvent tariffs. As of November 2019, the cumulative trade surplus of nine emerging Asian economies (excluding China) with the US had increased to approximately USD 167 billion. If trade surpluses with the US continue to widen, the relevant Asian economies could become the next targets of the trade war; for example, the US government imposed hefty tariffs of up to 456% on steel imports from Vietnam in July 2019. 7 In view of this, despite the Sino-US trade truce, the regional trade outlook remains highly uncertain. Chart 2.9 Goods Trade Surplus with the US Over the past decade, deepening international financial market integration has led to a significant increase in global cross-border portfolio investment flows. A recent study shows that up to 70% of these cross-border investment flows are driven by index-driven funds. 8 Index-driven funds include not only funds that closely track investment indices (commonly known as passive funds) but also actively managed funds that benchmark against investment indices. 9 By bringing in overseas investors that the relevant economies would otherwise be unable to attract or reach, these funds help promote the financial market development of emerging market economies. Consequently, such funds enable emerging market economies to diversify their investor base, contributing to the long-term growth and stability of the markets. However, is there really a free lunch? Regarding passive bond funds, there are market concerns that such fund investments may weaken the financial discipline of the corporate bond issuers they invest in, thereby leading to high leverage levels among the relevant enterprises. 10 Furthermore, it has been suggested that the growth of index-driven funds in recent years has exacerbated the volatility of global portfolio investment flows, making emerging market economies—which are already highly sensitive to global factors and affected by other common factors—even more vulnerable. 11 This box assesses the impact of index-driven investments on financial stability with respect to these two propositions. Passive bond funds allocate their investment capital to the relevant bonds according to the weights of the constituent bonds in the benchmark index. Therefore, compared to actively managed bond funds, the mechanical investment decisions adopted by passive bond funds may leave the issuers of index constituent bonds lacking the incentive to act in the interests of fund investors. 13 Worse still, from a financial stability perspective, such behavior may fuel excessive borrowing, bringing significant credit and debt-servicing risks to the corporate sectors of emerging market economies, whose leverage ratios have risen sharply since the global financial crisis (Chart B1.1). Chart B1.1 Corporate Leverage in Emerging Market Economies Using the weights of enterprises from various emerging market economies in a mainstream index tracking emerging market corporate bonds as an estimate of the passive bond fund investments in their bonds, 14 we find that an increase in such investments will push up the long-term (rather than short-term) leverage ratios of the corporate issuers of the relevant bonds. The solid blue bars in Chart B1.2 represent the estimated impact. In addition to promoting the development of corporate bond markets in emerging market economies, the expanded long-term bond investor base brought about by passive bond funds is also conducive to the development of emerging market enterprises. We also find that the aforementioned effect only has a significant impact on emerging market enterprises with sounder fundamentals (especially those with stronger debt-servicing capabilities and lower leverage ratios) (the solid green bars in Chart B1.2). Facing higher costs of financial distress, highly leveraged enterprises or those with poorer debt-servicing capabilities seem unlikely to fall further into the debt trap as a result of passive bond fund investments. In conclusion, the above study shows that the growth of passive bond fund investments may not substantially increase the debt-servicing risks of the corporate sectors in emerging market economies.

Hong Kong's economy contracted in the second half of 2019 and entered its first recession since 2009, dragged down by weakened private consumption, reduced investment expenditure, and poor export performance. Economic performance in 2020 is expected to face significant challenges, and the recent coronavirus epidemic has also posed substantial downside risks. The economic outlook is being affected by numerous uncertainties and risks, including the slowdown in global economic growth, China-US trade relations, the economic performance of Mainland China, and the development of local social incidents. Given the various headwinds facing the economy, the unemployment rate will likely climb further in 2020. Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease somewhat, although the outlook faces both potential upside and downside risks.  The Hong Kong economy contracted significantly in the second half of 2019. On a year-on-year basis, real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) contracted by 2.8% and 2.9% in the third and fourth quarters respectively (Table 3.A). Dragged down by the economic contraction in the second half of the year, the economy contracted by 1.2% for the whole year, worse than the 2.9% growth in 2018, marking the first annual contraction recorded since the 2009 global financial crisis.  Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth rate and contributions of major expenditure components  On a quarter-to-quarter basis, economic activities slowed down significantly in the second half of the year (Chart 3.1). Specifically, real GDP fell by 0.4%, 3.0%, and 0.3% in the second, third, and fourth quarters respectively, indicating that the economy had entered a recession. Domestically, private consumption was the main factor dragging down GDP in the third quarter. Local social incidents severely affected consumption activities, thereby weakening the economic outlook and dampening consumer sentiment, causing private consumption to contract significantly starting from the third quarter. 33 Due to increased economic uncertainties and deteriorating business sentiment, overall investment expenditure remained weak and dragged down GDP in the fourth quarter. 34 Externally, with the escalation of China-US trade frictions, weakening global economic growth, and a sharp plunge in visitor arrivals, Hong Kong's external trade performance remained sluggish (Chart 3.2). 35 Under the impact of a sharp contraction in exports of services, net exports dragged down GDP in the third quarter, but provided support to GDP growth in the fourth quarter, partly reflecting an improvement in the goods trade balance.  Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports  Given the immense headwinds facing the economy, the Government rolled out multiple rounds of measures between August and December 2019 to alleviate the financial burden on the public, safeguard jobs, and support enterprises, particularly supporting small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and severely hit sectors such as retail, food services, transport, and tourism. 36 To allow banks more space to step up their support for the local economy and help mitigate the economic cycle, the HKMA announced on October 14 a reduction of the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) ratio for banks from 2.5% to 2.0%, thereby enabling banks to release an additional HK$200 billion to HK$300 billion of lending capacity to enterprises, including SMEs.  Hong Kong's economic performance is expected to face significant challenges in 2020, and the epidemic has recently brought substantial downside risks. As some sectors have yet to recover from the disruptions caused by the social incidents, the epidemic will deal a double blow to these sectors. However, a series of countercyclical measures announced in the 2020-21 Budget can provide relief to households and enterprises (especially SMEs), including the disbursement of a one-off cash payout to adult permanent residents and the provision of a concessionary low-interest loan with a 100% Government guarantee for enterprises under the SME Financing Guarantee Scheme. 37 The HKMA further reduced the CCyB ratio for banks from 2.0% to 1.0% on March 16, 2020, which will allow banks more space to step up their support for the local economy, especially for sectors and individuals facing greater pressure in the near term due to the impact of the epidemic.  Analyzed by GDP components, private consumption and investment will likely remain weak due to fragile consumer and business sentiment. Although government consumption will support economic growth, public investment expenditure is expected to be relatively subdued as some major infrastructure projects are completed. On the external front, the phase one China-US trade agreement is expected to have a slight positive impact on the local economy in the near term. 38 However, weak global economic growth and trade activities will continue to drag down Hong Kong's external trade performance. In particular, the coronavirus outbreak may lead to supply chain disruptions in the region and a slowdown in cross-border economic activities (such as tourism), thereby constraining Hong Kong's export performance.  The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2020 to range between -1.5% and 0.5%, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is -1.5%. This weak economic outlook is affected by the numerous uncertainties and risks mentioned in the preceding chapters.  The labor market faced greater pressure in the second half of 2019 and early 2020. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate rose from a multi-year low of 2.8% in June 2019 to 3.3% in December 2019, and climbed further to 3.7% in February 2020 (Chart 3.3). Among them, the unemployment rate for the retail, accommodation, and food services sectors surged to a near-decade high of 6.1%, partly reflecting the severe blow dealt by the social incidents. 39 As economic momentum weakened, total employment fell by 0.5% year-on-year in the second half of 2019 and continued to decline to 3,768,800 in February 2020. The decline in employment was mainly driven by the trade, wholesale, retail, accommodation, food services, and construction sectors. Real payroll also fell by 0.3% year-on-year in the third quarter. Looking ahead, in view of the aforementioned weak economic outlook, the labor market will continue to face more challenges, and the unemployment rate is highly likely to climb further. Box 3 will explore the recent developments and near-term outlook of the labor market in greater detail.  Chart 3.3 Labor market conditions  Local inflationary pressures continued to build up until the third quarter of 2019, mainly due to the impact of rising fresh pork prices; thereafter, as economic activities weakened, inflation momentum also gradually slowed down. On a year-on-year basis, the Underlying Composite Consumer Price Index (CPI) grew by 3.3% in the third quarter, while the increase moderated slightly to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. The annualized 3-month rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, also eased from a peak of 4.7% in August 2019 to 2.1% in January 2020. The slowdown in inflation momentum was due to reduced price pressures across various CPI components. For tradable goods, underlying food inflation remained visible due to the surge in fresh pork prices, but price pressures on consumer goods such as clothing and footwear, as well as durable goods, remained mild. For services, with the slower growth in newly let private housing rentals earlier, the increase in the rental component of the CPI also showed a downward trend (Chart 3.5). Labor cost pressures rose slightly but remained at a moderate level in recent quarters (Chart 3.6).  Chart 3.4 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation Chart 3.5 Composite CPI rental component and market rentals Chart 3.6 Unit labor cost  Local inflationary pressures are expected to ease somewhat in the near term. Domestically, the weak economic conditions and a widened negative output gap will continue to exert downward pressure on local inflation. As private housing rentals continue to soften, the housing rental component of inflation should ease further. Externally, imported inflation is expected to remain mild due to weak global economic growth and soft energy prices. Market consensus forecasts the headline inflation rate for 2020 to range between 0.6% and 3.7%, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate at 2.5% and the headline inflation rate at 1.7%. This inflation outlook is subject to both upside and downside risk factors. On the one hand, given that the estimated negative output gap has widened since the third quarter of 2019, if the economic deterioration is more severe than expected (for example, due to the persistence of the coronavirus epidemic), it may further suppress inflation. On the other hand, if the disruption to the fresh pork supply becomes more severe, it will bring upside pressure to inflation.  Despite the visible slowdown in the Hong Kong economy, the unemployment rate remained at a low level of 2.8-2.9% in the first nine months of 2019. It was only as the social incidents persisted that the unemployment rate climbed more visibly to 3.3% by the end of 2019. Affected by the coronavirus epidemic, the labor market will face greater headwinds in 2020. Against this backdrop, this Box analyzes the recent developments and near-term outlook of the labor market, including exploring why the overall labor market was largely resilient (with the unemployment rate remaining virtually unchanged) in the first three quarters of 2019, and what implications this has for future developments. This article also examines some risk factors that could lead to a sharp rise in the unemployment rate. It is worth noting that the unemployment rate is a lagging indicator, partly because adjusting labor demand entails costs. In fact, the unemployment rate often lags behind the year-on-year growth rate of real GDP by about two to three quarters (Chart B3.1). This lagging nature can explain why the unemployment rate remained low at around 2.9% when real economic activities deteriorated sharply in the third quarter.  Chart B3.1 Real GDP growth rate and unemployment rate  On the labor demand side, although China-US trade tensions and local social incidents dealt a heavy blow to employment in the trade and retail and tourism-related sectors respectively, some major sectors were still able to support the overall labor market. Specifically, employment in the financing, business, public administration, social and personal services sectors continued to grow in 2019, partly offsetting the impact of the decline in employment in the trade and retail sectors (Chart B3.2). Despite the economy entering a recession, Hong Kong's financial system remained robust, and financial activities in terms of fintech development and initial public offerings (IPOs) were also very active. These factors may have helped support the employment market in the financing and business services sectors. In addition, the public administration, social and personal services sectors, which include education, human health and social work activities, appear to be less sensitive to the economic cycle. Correlation coefficient analysis shows that while employment in many sectors is highly correlated with real GDP, the response of the public administration, social and personal services sectors to the economic cycle is more neutral. In other words, even if the economy slows down, employment in these sectors may not be subject to significant cyclical impacts.  Chart B3.2 Changes in employment by sector in 2019  On the labor supply side, the labor force participation rate 40 declined from 61.2% in 2018 to 60.5% in 2019, providing a buffer against the rise in the unemployment rate. Chart B3.3 shows the various supply and demand factors affecting the change in the unemployment rate (blue line). As shown in the chart, the labor force participation rate (green bars) exerted downward pressure on the unemployment rate in 2019. 41 On the other hand, the increase in employment in the first half of 2019 (purple bars) also helped suppress the unemployment rate. However, with the significant economic contraction in the second half of the year, the decline in employment exerted upside pressure on the unemployment rate. Overall, although employment declined during the economic recession, the lower labor force participation rate helped mitigate the upward pressure on the unemployment rate in the second half of 2019.  Chart B3.3 Factors contributing to changes in the unemployment rate  Some changes in the structure of the labor market are also worth noting. In particular, the increased proportion of voluntary part-time employees may help companies retain staff. In fact, while the proportions of self-employed persons and underemployed persons in total employment have declined to 6% and 1% respectively in recent years, the number of voluntary part-time employees has continued to rise, becoming the second largest group in the total employed population (about 7% in 2017). 42 Therefore, companies may be able to retain or hire more staff by adjusting the working hours of part-time employees. Our calculations show that average weekly working hours have decreased, falling from a recent high of 48 hours in 2010 to about 44 hours currently, partly reflecting the presence of more part-time workers in the current employed population.

The Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate has strengthened since October, with upward momentum further increasing in December, keeping the HKD exchange rate on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months. The strong demand for the HKD was partly driven by equity-related demand, and partly due to the unwinding of short HKD positions prompted by tightening liquidity towards the year-end. Overall, the Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. Although market sentiment triggered by the coronavirus outbreak under an uncertain external environment may lead to increased volatility in fund flows, Hong Kong has massive foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, making it capable of withstanding capital outflow pressures without affecting local financial stability. Supported by increased equity-related demand for the HKD (including Initial Public Offerings (IPOs)), the HKD exchange rate has gradually strengthened since mid-October (Chart 4.1). Entering December, the upward momentum of the HKD further strengthened. From mid-December to February, the HKD exchange rate remained on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone. The strengthening of the HKD exchange rate was partly due to buoyant IPO activities, and partly due to the unwinding of short HKD positions prompted by tightening liquidity towards the year-end. After the Lunar New Year holidays, liquidity conditions eased somewhat, and the HKD exchange rate softened slightly, closing at 7.7956 on February 28. Overall, HKD trading continued to be smooth and orderly during the review period. As neither the strong-side nor the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered during the review period, the Aggregate Balance remained unchanged at around HK$54 billion (Chart 4.2). Chart 4.1 HKD Exchange Rate Chart 4.2 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes The Nominal Effective Exchange Rate Index of the HKD broadly tracked the movements of the US dollar and edged up during the review period (Chart 4.3). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was very small and thus had a limited impact on the Real Effective Exchange Rate Index of the HKD, the movement of the Real Effective Exchange Rate Index broadly tracked that of the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate Index. Chart 4.3 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates When measuring fund flows in Hong Kong, it is necessary to distinguish between two distinct but interrelated concepts of fund flows: (1) HKD fund flows; and (2) cross-border fund flows. HKD fund flows focus on the currency dimension of fund flows, which helps assess monetary stability, particularly under the Linked Exchange Rate System. On the other hand, cross-border fund flows focus on the geographical movement of funds through the Hong Kong banking system, which helps assess the stability of Hong Kong's overall financial system. The two concepts of fund flows require different monitoring indicators. When monitoring HKD fund flows, attention should be paid to the HKD exchange rate and the Aggregate Balance. If the public or investors convert a large amount of their HKD assets into foreign currency assets, the demand for the HKD will naturally decline, leading to a weakening of the HKD exchange rate. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, if the HKD exchange rate weakens to the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking rate of HK$7.85 to US$1, the HKMA stands ready to buy HKD at the request of banks, and the Aggregate Balance will subsequently decrease. Since April 2019, the Aggregate Balance has remained broadly unchanged, and the HKD exchange rate has been on the strong side of the Convertibility Zone in recent months; therefore, no significant fund outflows from the HKD were observed during the review period. When monitoring cross-border fund flows, total bank deposits in Hong Kong serve as a useful indicator. When there are massive capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system, bank deposits will inevitably decrease. During the review period, total deposits grew at a moderate pace, indicating that there were no significant cross-border fund outflows. The Hong Kong foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner, indicating that the impact of the coronavirus outbreak on the local monetary environment remains limited. However, we need to closely monitor the risks brought about by the coronavirus outbreak. Hong Kong has massive foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system; the HKMA has the capability, resources, and determination to cope with capital outflows and maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. Despite the uncertain external environment and the slowdown in the local economy, Hong Kong's monetary environment remained relatively accommodative during the review period. The HKD Monetary Base remained large, rising by 4.0% since the end of June to HK$1,689.4 billion at the end of January 2020 (Chart 4.4). As the Convertibility Undertaking was not triggered during this period, the Aggregate Balance remained broadly unchanged at around HK$54 billion. Other components of the Monetary Base, including outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, Certificates of Indebtedness, and government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, increased steadily. Chart 4.4 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, broad HKD money supply indicators remained broadly stable. Broad HKD money supply (HKD M3) grew by 3.5% in the first half of 2019, and then edged up by 0.2% during the seven-month period since the end of June 2019. Counterpart analysis shows that the growth in HKD M3 since the end of June mainly reflected an increase in banks' net foreign currency assets and a rise in the Monetary Base (driven by increases in Certificates of Indebtedness and government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation) (Chart 4.5). During the seven-month period since the end of June, HKD deposits (the major component of HKD M3) remained broadly unchanged (Chart 4.6). Among HKD deposits, time deposits continued to grow moderately, partly reflecting the rise in HKD deposit rates. Chart 4.5 Changes in HKD M3 and its Counterparts During the seven-month period since the end of June 2019, foreign currency deposits grew moderately by 2.3% (Chart 4.6), mainly driven by US dollar deposits, which increased by 3.5% during this period. Other foreign currency deposits fell by 1.0% over the same period, among which renminbi deposits recorded a slight decline in HKD terms. Overall, total deposits with authorized institutions grew steadily by 1.2% since the end of June. Supported by the increase in total deposits, Hong Kong's total broad money supply also rose at a relatively stable pace, with total money supply M2 and M3 increasing by 1.6% and 1.5% respectively since the end of June (Chart 4.7). As monthly monetary statistics may be subject to volatility due to various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), these statistics should be interpreted with caution. Chart 4.6 Deposits with Authorized Institutions by Currency Chart 4.7 Total Broad Money Supply (M2) Although the monetary environment remained relatively accommodative, short-term Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) experienced volatility, reflecting seasonal liquidity demand and increased capital market activities since the fourth quarter of 2019, particularly the active IPO activities in the Hong Kong stock market. The overnight HIBOR occasionally exhibited larger fluctuations in late October and mid-November (Chart 4.8). 44 During the review period, other short-term HIBORs generally increased. Subscriptions for large-scale IPOs can exert significant pressure on the overnight HIBOR. Empirical analysis in Box 4 shows that market attention to future IPO activities also affects the 3-month HIBOR. This situation occurs if market participants anticipate the future subscription closing dates of large-scale IPOs and prepare medium-term funding in advance for early deployment. Chart 4.8 HKD and USD Interbank Offered Rates As for the HKD yield curve, it shifted downwards tracking the US dollar yield curve. Compared to the end of June 2019, the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 60 basis points to 1.04% on February 28, 2020 (Chart 4.9). Meanwhile, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds fell by 50 basis points to 1.00% over the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate and Average Interest Rate for New Mortgage Loans At the retail level, the composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of HKD funds for retail banks, gradually rose from 0.94% at the end of July 2019 to 1.01% at the end of January 2020. This increase mainly reflected that banks continued to raise promotional deposit rates to attract deposit funds, leading to a rise in the weighted HKD deposit rate. At the end of October 2019, following the downward adjustment of the target range for the US federal funds rate, a number of retail banks lowered their best lending rates by 12.5 basis points. Consequently, the best lending rates of retail banks currently range from 5.00% to 5.50%. Regarding mortgage loans, for HIBOR-based mortgage loans, major banks raised the interest rate caps determined by the best lending rate, causing the average interest rate for new mortgage loans to rise to around 2.63% in October. 45 The best lending rates in the market have been lowered since November, and the average mortgage interest rate subsequently declined slightly to 2.53% in January 2020. In response to the evolving risks posed by the coronavirus outbreak to US economic activity, and to support the US Federal Reserve in achieving its policy goals, the Federal Reserve lowered the target range for the federal funds rate by a total of 150 basis points to 0-0.25% on March 3 (US time) and March 15 (US time). Although HIBORs track US dollar interest rates in the long run, short-term HIBORs may be influenced by local factors that could affect HKD demand, such as local IPO activities. With the Aggregate Balance of the banking system decreasing since April 2018, the sensitivity of HIBORs to changes in HKD funding supply and demand may have increased. However, this does not mean that the current Aggregate Balance level of HK$54 billion is insufficient to meet the needs of interbank payment and settlement. In fact, the Hong Kong interbank market has been operating in an orderly manner. In the event of short-term liquidity tightness, banks can utilize the liquidity facilities provided by the HKMA. In view of the potential escalation of the US-China trade conflict, the offshore and onshore renminbi (RMB) exchange rates weakened significantly in late August and September 2019, with the offshore RMB against the US dollar dropping to a ten-year low of 7.19 on September 2 (Chart 4.10). Entering October, market expectations of the resumption of US-China trade talks reversed the RMB depreciation trend. The offshore and onshore RMB strengthened in the fourth quarter and, following the signing of the phase one trade agreement between the US and China, briefly breached the 6.9 level in mid-January 2020. However, since late January, due to the coronavirus outbreak, the offshore and onshore RMB have once again faced weakening pressure. The offshore RMB traded at a discount to the onshore RMB for most of the time between May and August, and generally at a premium in the latter part of 2019. The discount briefly widened at the end of January 2020, but the spread between the two remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and Offshore RMB Exchange Rates Despite the volatility in the RMB exchange rate, liquidity conditions in the offshore RMB interbank market remained broadly stable. During the review period, the 3-month offshore RMB HIBOR continued to hover between 3% and 4% (Chart 4.11). The overnight offshore RMB HIBOR experienced brief volatility in late August and late November due to the Morgan Stanley Capital International (MSCI) A-share adjustments, and in late January 2020 approaching the Lunar New Year holidays.

Due to increased uncertainties in the global and local economic environments, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong recorded a slight decline in the second half of 2019. Nevertheless, the capital and liquidity positions of the Hong Kong banking sector remained strong and robust by international standards. Asset quality remained at a healthy level by historical standards. Although the growth rate of total loans slowed down in the second half of last year, it still outpaced deposit growth during the review period. Correspondingly, the average loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies and the Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions both increased. However, given that the Aggregate Balance of the banking system was at a stable level and deposits remained broadly stable, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust. Looking ahead, the Hong Kong banking sector will continue to face multiple downside risks, including uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, future US-China trade relations, geopolitical tensions, and local social incidents. Given the continuous rise in corporate leverage and personal debt burdens, banks should prudently assess the impact on the asset quality of their loan portfolios should these risk factors intensify.  In the second half of 2019, the aggregate pre-tax operating profit 59 of retail banks fell slightly by 1.5% compared with the same period in 2018. Correspondingly, the return on assets edged down to 1.13% in the second half of 2019, lower than the 1.23% in the same period of 2018 (Chart 5.1). Although the net interest margin of retail banks narrowed slightly from 1.67% in the second half of 2018 to 1.63% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.2), the net interest income of retail banks continued to record moderate growth during the review period. However, both loan impairment charges and operating expenses of retail banks increased, leading to a slight decline in profitability.  Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks  Despite the US federal funds target rate being lowered three times by 25 basis points each in the second half of 2019, the Hong Kong dollar wholesale funding market has not yet seen significant downward pressure. Conversely, driven by multiple local factors (including seasonal funding demand, increased liquidity demand due to large-scale initial public offerings, and tighter interbank market liquidity conditions), short-term Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates (HIBORs) have been on an upward trend since the fourth quarter of 2019. Meanwhile, longer-term HIBORs remained broadly stable during the review period, with the three-month HIBOR staying at 2.43% at the end of 2019, close to the level six months ago (blue line in Chart 5.3). At the retail level, as Hong Kong dollar savings deposit rates remained close to zero, there was limited room for retail banks to follow suit in cutting interest rates after the US lowered its policy rate. 60 On the other hand, as Hong Kong dollar liquidity in the banking system tightened during the review period, banks continued to compete for long-term stable deposit funding. 61 Reflecting the increase in the weighted funding cost of Hong Kong dollar deposits, the composite interest rate (an indicator measuring the average Hong Kong dollar funding cost of retail banks) rose gradually from 0.95% six months ago to 1.09% at the end of 2019, although it remained at a relatively low level by historical standards (green line in Chart 5.3).  Chart 5.3 Interest rates  From a broader perspective, given that the decline in US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong offset the slight increase in their Hong Kong dollar funding costs, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong edged down by 14 basis points in the second half of 2019 (Chart 5.4). During the review period, banks' net interest income benefited from the slight decline in their overall funding costs and the relatively high level of HIBORs, providing support to banking sector profitability over the same period. Since June 2019, all licensed banks subject to the new local interest rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB) framework have been submitting returns under the new framework, while exempted licensed banks have continued to submit returns under the existing interest rate risk framework. The overall funding costs and maturity have been calculated as a weighted average based on the relevant figures of these two categories of licensed banks. Therefore, figures from June 2019 onwards cannot be directly compared with those of previous months.  Looking ahead, multiple downside risk factors in the external and local environments will continue to cloud the profitability outlook of banks. Relevant factors include uncertainties arising from the spread of the coronavirus, the future direction of US-China trade relations, and the escalation of geopolitical tensions. The intensification of these risk factors may dampen the already weak global economic growth momentum and reduce the demand for bank credit. Given the widespread adoption of accommodative monetary policies by major central banks, the global low interest rate environment is likely to persist, which may exert pressure on banks' future net interest margins. At the local level, local social incidents since mid-2019 have continued to hit business investment and market confidence. Against the backdrop of an already weak economic environment, if the situation persists or even further intensifies in the future, it may lead to a deterioration in the credit demand outlook and banks' asset quality.  Regarding overall market development, following the granting of eight virtual bank licences by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the Hong Kong banking sector has begun to roll out virtual banking services. As these new market participants may seek to increase their market share by launching more convenient products and more attractive deposit rates to attract new customers, this may exert upward pressure on the funding costs of incumbent banks. Although the short-term impact may remain mild as the current business scale of virtual banks is still limited, the long-term impact may depend on whether incumbent banks will accelerate the adoption of Fintech to maintain competitiveness. The results of Feature 5 show that the degree of Fintech adoption by Hong Kong banks is statistically correlated with improvements in their cost efficiency and profitability levels.  The capitalization of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above minimum international standards. As of the end of 2019, the consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions rose further to 20.7% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio also increased to 18.5%, of which 16.5% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital.  Chart 5.5 Capitalization of locally incorporated authorized institutions  In addition to the risk-based capital adequacy ratios, there is also the non-risk-based leverage ratio requirement under Basel III to restrict excessive leverage in the banking system. The leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions remained at a robust level of 8.2% at the end of 2019, exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 3% (Chart 5.6).  Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated authorized institutions  Measured by the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) 65 requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average LCR of Category 1 institutions increased from 152.8% in the second quarter of 2019 to 159.9% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio (LMR) of Category 2 institutions also rose moderately from 54.6% in the second quarter of 2019 to around 56.3% in the fourth quarter of 2019, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%.  Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio  The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) 66, as one of the liquidity standards under Basel III, indicates that the funding position of authorized institutions is stable. The average NSFR of Category 1 institutions remained at a high level of 131.7% in the fourth quarter of 2019 (Chart 5.8), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. The average Core Funding Ratio (CFR) of Category 2A institutions remained at a high level of 134.5%, also exceeding the statutory minimum requirement of 75% applicable in 2019. The ample liquidity and robust funding positions of authorized institutions indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding various liquidity shocks.  Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio  Customer deposits remained the major source of funding for authorized institutions, reflecting that the banking system maintained a stable funding structure. At the end of 2019, the share of customer deposits in the total liabilities of all authorized institutions remained broadly unchanged, edging down to 56.3% from 56.4% six months ago (Chart 5.9).  Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all authorized institutions  The average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio of all authorized institutions increased from 89.3% at the end of June 2019 to 90.3% at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.10), as the level of Hong Kong dollar loans and advances remained broadly stable while deposits fell slightly during the review period. 67 Meanwhile, as the growth rate of foreign currency loans outpaced that of deposits, the average foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio also rose from 58.9% to 60.4% over the same period. Overall, the average loan-to-deposit ratio for all currencies of all authorized institutions increased from 74.5% at the end of June 2019 to 75.4% at the end of the same year. Given that the Aggregate Balance of the banking system has remained stable since April 2019 and deposits have remained broadly stable, there were no noticeable signs of significant fund outflows from the Hong Kong dollar or the Hong Kong banking system during the review period.
