We estimate that under an assumed shock of a 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks would be equivalent to 1.56% of their total capital base at the end of 2019 (Chart 5.11).  Chart 5.11 Impact of Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rate shocks on locally incorporated licensed banks  Against the backdrop of US-China trade tensions, a global economic slowdown, and ongoing local social incidents, bank credit growth slowed in the second half of 2019 after a moderate rebound in the first half of the year. On a half-yearly basis, loan growth (measured by the change in total loans and advances of all authorized institutions) grew moderately by 4.2% in the first half of 2019, before slowing to 2.4% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The slowdown in loan growth was due to the moderating growth trends in both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong during the review period. Domestic loans and loans for use outside Hong Kong grew by 2.5% and 2.2% respectively in the second half of 2019, lower than the increases of 4.5% and 3.5% in the first half. Nevertheless, total loan growth for the whole year of 2019 still rose moderately to 6.7%, higher than the 4.4% for the whole year of 2018.

The rollout of COVID-19 vaccines has brought hope for reopening the economy, boosting the global growth outlook. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing policies, financial markets have repeatedly hit new highs. However, the global outlook remains clouded by uncertainties, and the pace of recovery is expected to be uneven across economies. In the medium term, the disconnect between financial markets and the real economy, high debt levels, and the long-lasting economic scarring caused by the pandemic will be challenges facing policymakers going forward. The Hong Kong dollar foreign exchange and money markets continued to operate smoothly and in an orderly manner. The Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar stayed close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, driven mainly by equity-related demand. During the review period, total deposits increased, and there were no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Partly reflecting weak economic activities and reduced credit demand caused by the recurring pandemic, total loans in the banking sector declined slightly in the second half of the year, although a slight increase was still recorded for 2020 as a whole. Meanwhile, the residential property market remained broadly stable. Looking ahead, uncertainties surrounding the pace of economic recovery and lingering geopolitical risks will continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic will weaken the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of related downside risk factors on asset quality. Global economic growth rebounded in the third quarter of 2020 as various regions reopened their economies, but global growth slowed again as COVID-19 infection numbers resurged from the fourth quarter onwards. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development in late 2020, the market expects the pandemic to eventually end, which is conducive to the global economy returning to normal and accelerating growth. Coupled with continued fiscal and monetary easing policies, global financial markets rose to new highs in early 2021, although signs of a disconnect with the real economy began to emerge. Against this backdrop, uncertainties will continue to cloud the global economic outlook. Whether vaccines can be widely distributed remains to be seen. At the same time, supply bottlenecks and earlier aggressive easing policies may lead to higher-than-expected inflation, which in turn may prompt central banks to taper monetary easing earlier than expected, ending financial markets' expectations of a "lower for longer" monetary policy. In the long run, policymakers need to assess the costs and benefits of extending relief measures and address the numerous economic legacies triggered by the pandemic, including high global debt and long-lasting economic scarring. In the East Asian region, supported by a rebound in export demand, domestic Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth improved in the second half of 2020. Amid increased risk appetite, portfolio capital inflows to the region rebounded, and yield-seeking activities re-emerged. Despite these positive developments, the East Asian region still faces lingering uncertainties brought about by the pandemic. First, in the global competition for vaccine procurement, less developed economies in the region may lag behind advanced economies in achieving herd immunity, hindering the recovery of their tourism and service sectors. Second, variables may arise in the supply, coverage, or effectiveness of vaccines, which, coupled with the weakening fiscal positions of governments in the region, could sour market sentiment and trigger capital flow reversals. As for Mainland China, with consumption activities gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. For 2020 as a whole, the Mainland economy grew by 2.3%, making it the only major economy to record positive growth. Looking ahead, the economic outlook still depends largely on the development of the pandemic and changes in Sino-US tensions. The latest consensus forecasts indicate that the Mainland economy will grow by 8.4% in 2021. The Renminbi (RMB) recorded several months of depreciation in early 2020, and subsequently strengthened for the rest of the year amid an accelerated economic recovery, a weaker US dollar, and strong capital inflows into the Mainland bond market. Detailed studies show that during the COVID-19 outbreak, fundamental factors rather than market sentiment played a more important role in driving RMB exchange rate fluctuations (for details, please refer to Box 1). The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020, but real GDP remained well below pre-pandemic levels. With a slight increase in domestic demand and a further expansion in goods exports, seasonally adjusted real GDP began to rebound in the third quarter, ending the previous five consecutive quarters of contraction. The year-on-year contraction of real GDP also narrowed significantly from 9% in the first half of 2020 to about 3% in the second half. However, for 2020 as a whole, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and following a 1.2% contraction in 2019, it marked the first time in history that a decline was recorded for two consecutive years. The latest GDP data by sector show that the contraction in consumption- and tourism-related sectors under the pandemic was worse than that of the overall economy. To cope with the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two more rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund in the second half of 2020 to help sectors and citizens affected by the pandemic and to enhance Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capabilities. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the recent 2021-22 Budget to boost the economy, including the issuance of a one-off HK$5,000 electronic consumption voucher and the provision of a 100% Personal Loan Guarantee Scheme for the unemployed. The HKMA, together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced in March 2021 the extension of the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme to October of the same year, and announced the extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the Scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate the cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers. COVID-19 vaccines are expected to bring economic activities back to normal, and the local economy is expected to resume positive growth in 2021 (for the year as a whole), but the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties such as the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination takes time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, which can provide support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their mass vaccination programmes. The Government forecasts real GDP growth of between 3.5% and 5.5% in 2021, while the average growth forecast by international organizations and private sector analysts is 4.4%. Labor market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The unemployment rate climbed further, reaching a 17-year high of 7.2% in February 2021, while the underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. To cope with the continuously deteriorating labor market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund to provide time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain employees. Following the end of the Employment Support Scheme, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support sectors hard hit by the pandemic. In the short term, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Box 2 explores the potential impact of the rise and fall of inbound tourism on the local labor market. Local inflationary pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell significantly to 0.3% and 0.2% year-on-year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further declined to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively. The annualized 3-month rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, has remained at a low level despite slight fluctuations in recent months. As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, local inflationary pressures are likely to remain mild in the near term; in particular, local inflation will continue to be contained by the slower growth in newly let private residential rentals earlier. The market consensus forecasts the headline inflation rate for 2021 to be at a moderate level of 1.4%, while the Government forecasts the underlying and headline inflation rates for 2021 to be 1.0% and 1.6% respectively. The Hong Kong dollar against the US dollar stayed close to the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking level, driven mainly by equity-related funding demand, including that from buoyant initial public offering (IPO) activities and Southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. Fund-raising activities remained active in the first two months of 2021, keeping the Hong Kong dollar persistently strong. During the review period, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered 47 times in September and October 2020, with HK$263.3 billion of funds flowing into the Hong Kong dollar. For 2020 as a whole, the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking was triggered a total of 85 times, with a cumulative inflow of HK$383.5 billion. Overall, Hong Kong dollar trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Analyzed from a geographical perspective, total deposits increased during the review period, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. Although uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and ongoing Sino-US tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, and is therefore well-equipped to withstand capital flow volatility. With the Aggregate Balance increasing as a result of the triggering of the strong-side Convertibility Undertaking, Hong Kong dollar interbank offered rates (HIBORs) generally remained at extremely low levels. The composite interest rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.23% at the end of February 2021. Due to the lower funding costs, the average lending rate for new mortgage loans also dropped from 2.02% in June to 1.56% in January. On the other hand, the best lending rates of major retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Following the strengthening of the onshore Renminbi (CNY) exchange rate, the offshore Renminbi (CNH) has appreciated against the US dollar since late May 2020. For most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium over the CNY exchange rate; the average premium in the fourth quarter was about 100 pips, which remained moderate by historical standards. Hong Kong's offshore RMB liquidity pool continued to expand in the second half of 2020, with the outstanding amount of RMB customer deposits and certificates of deposit increasing to RMB 826.3 billion at the end of January 2021. As for other RMB businesses, RMB bank loans in Hong Kong decreased, while RMB trade settlement grew. The average daily turnover of the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system remained at a high level of RMB 1,191.5 billion for 2020 as a whole. Hong Kong possesses highly efficient financial infrastructure, providing investors with numerous cross-border fund flow channels connecting to the Mainland. With the continued opening up of the Mainland's capital account, increasing demand for RMB assets from international investors, and the deepening of regional economic and financial cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area initiative, Hong Kong's offshore RMB business is expected to benefit. Supported by the rally in global stock markets and active purchases of Hong Kong stocks by Mainland investors through the Southbound Stock Connect, the local stock market rebounded after a sharp correction at the beginning of the review period. The rally in global stock markets was driven by factors including unprecedented monetary easing measures adopted by major economies; market optimism over positive progress in vaccine development, which was seen as potentially helping to accelerate the recovery of economic activities; and a reduction in global geopolitical uncertainties. Against this backdrop, the Hang Seng Index recouped its losses after a sharp fall in 2020, rising by 15.1% during the review period, and briefly breached the 31,000-point mark in mid-February 2021, hitting a 32-month high. Supported by stable issuance volumes, the Hong Kong dollar and offshore RMB bond markets continued to expand in the second half of 2020. After experiencing significant net capital outflows in the first half of 2020, market confidence recovered rapidly as governments worldwide rolled out unprecedented economic stimulus measures, leading to a rebound in bond fund inflows into the local market. Although bond yields rebounded moderately during the same period, global bond yields, including those in Hong Kong, still hovered near historical lows.

With breakthroughs in vaccine development, the market expects the novel coronavirus pandemic to eventually come to an end, enabling the global economy to accelerate its growth going forward. Coupled with the expectation of a "lower for longer" global monetary policy, investors were not deterred by the resurgence of the pandemic in late 2020, and financial markets reached new highs in early 2021. However, the high expectations of the financial markets are somewhat disconnected from the still-challenging macroeconomic environment. Should the strength of the economic recovery fall short of expectations, or if policy support is withdrawn earlier than expected (for example, due to higher-than-expected inflation), asset prices may experience volatility. Looking ahead, policymakers will face the dilemma of when to withdraw policy support, as well as the need to address the many legacy issues left by the pandemic, including high debt levels and long-term economic scarring. Lingering uncertainties surrounding the pandemic continue to cast a shadow over the economic recovery in the East Asian region, and the slower-developing emerging market economies in the region may face greater challenges in vaccine procurement and distribution. Any setbacks in the progress of vaccination programmes could reverse the current optimism, destabilising capital inflows and financial markets. As for Mainland China, with consumption activities gradually returning to normal, the pace of economic recovery accelerated in the second half of 2020. Looking ahead, the economic growth outlook remains highly uncertain, depending to a large extent on the development of the pandemic and changes in Sino-US tensions. Therefore, the government announced that it would maintain a supportive policy stance and emphasized the importance of controlling systemic risks. Benefiting from the purchasing power released by the economic reopening, major economies mostly recorded better-than-expected real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth in the third quarter of 2020. However, since the fourth quarter, the number of novel coronavirus infections has climbed again, prompting governments to reinstate lockdown and social distancing measures, which once again weakened the global growth momentum. In late 2020, more transmissible mutant strains of the virus emerged and subsequently spread around the world, making the situation even more severe. Nevertheless, with breakthroughs in vaccine development and the approval of multiple vaccines for use in late 2020, the market expects the pandemic to eventually end, and the global economy to return to normal and accelerate its growth. Another driver supporting the global economic recovery comes from sustained policy stimulus measures, including the commitment by major central banks to a "lower for longer" monetary policy amid weak inflation, as well as continued fiscal easing measures in major advanced economies, particularly the fiscal stimulus packages passed by the US Congress in December 2020 and March 2021. Accordingly, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) revised its 2021 global GDP growth forecast upwards to 5.5% in January 2021, which is 0.3 percentage points higher than the forecast made in October 2020 (Chart 2.1). Chart 2.1 Real GDP growth forecasts made by the International Monetary Fund in January 2021 and October 2020 Against this backdrop, market optimism strengthened, and share prices of cyclical sectors that typically benefit from economic recovery rose, driving global share prices and valuations to new highs in early 2021 (Chart 2.2). Chart 2.2 12-month forward price-to-earnings ratios of major stock indices However, while financial markets performed strongly, the macroeconomic situation remains challenging. The disconnect between the two could lead to volatility in asset markets in the face of multiple risks. First, the prospect of bringing the pandemic under control depends on the widespread distribution of vaccines, which remains to be seen. As of mid-March 2021, the overall global vaccination rate remained low (Chart 2.3). Although there are global mechanisms (such as COVAX) to promote a more equitable distribution of vaccines, the problem of low vaccination rates in lower-income emerging market economies is expected to be more severe due to limited vaccine supplies. If the containment of the pandemic falls short of expectations, various regions may need to extend social distancing and other restrictive measures, thereby dampening the global recovery outlook. Chart 2.3 Proportion of the population having received at least one dose of vaccine in selected economies (as of 15 March 2021) Second, the rebound in financial markets is built on sustained monetary and fiscal policy support, especially the "lower for longer" monetary policy. However, there is a risk that support measures may be withdrawn at a faster-than-expected pace. For example, under the combined effects of supply bottlenecks, strong money and liquidity growth, and aggressive fiscal easing policies, inflation expectations in the US and Europe have already risen (Chart 2.4). If future inflation is stronger than expected, central banks may need to scale back their monetary easing policies, and higher-than-expected inflation data could also lead to greater volatility in financial markets. Chart 2.4 US and Euro area 5-year/5-year inflation-linked swap rates Third, there is significant uncertainty in future Sino-US relations. The wave of Sino-US "decoupling", particularly in the financial and technological sectors, has intensified since the outbreak of the pandemic. Given the increasingly tough stance of both the Democratic and Republican parties in the US towards Mainland China, this trend may not necessarily reverse under the Biden administration. Should Sino-US tensions escalate unexpectedly, it could trigger financial market turbulence in the future. Looking ahead, policymakers will need to face the dilemma of whether and when to withdraw pandemic support measures. While a premature withdrawal of such measures could jeopardize the economic recovery and create a "cliff effect", these measures are costly in the long run, including imposing fiscal burdens and delaying necessary post-pandemic resource reallocation, such as allowing "zombie companies" with unviable business models to survive with continued government support. In addition, policymakers must also address the many legacy issues left by the pandemic. First, due to declining corporate revenues and surging government expenditures, global debt levels rose sharply in 2020 (Chart 2.5). Although the problems brought about by the surge in debt may not be imminent given that global interest rates are currently at extremely low levels, the continuous accumulation of debt in the public and private sectors may raise market concerns about fiscal sustainability and financial stability. Chart 2.5 Global debt-to-GDP ratio Another legacy issue involves the potential long-term economic losses or permanent scarring caused by the pandemic. For example, elevated uncertainty may lead businesses to reduce investment, while workers suffering from long-term unemployment may permanently exit the labor market, resulting in a massive waste of human resources. In East Asia, real GDP growth stabilized in the second half of 2020 after a sharp plunge in the second quarter (Chart 2.6). The momentum of economic recovery mainly came from a rebound in exports, among which the export demand for electronics and technological equipment was the most robust. At the same time, the hardest-hit service sectors (such as tourism and consumer services that require face-to-face contact with customers) continued to struggle. Chart 2.6 East Asia: Real GDP growth in 2020 Despite the lingering uncertainties surrounding the economic recovery, portfolio investment flows have resumed. Since the second half of last year, the region has attracted more bond inflows due to improved market sentiment and higher yields relative to advanced economy bonds (Chart 2.7). With signs of economic recovery and the rollout of vaccine production plans, equity inflows into the East Asian region also accelerated in the last quarter of 2020. Regional currencies also appreciated correspondingly due to portfolio inflows, causing the Bloomberg JPMorgan Asia Dollar Index to rebound by about 10% from its lowest point in March last year. Chart 2.7 East Asia: Portfolio investment flows The East Asian region continues to face lingering uncertainties from the pandemic. First, although the rollout of vaccines brings hope to the region's hard-hit service sectors and economies, global competition for early batches of vaccines has driven up procurement costs, and vaccine distribution also poses challenges to the region's logistics and public health capacities. Therefore, slower-developing economies in the region may achieve herd immunity later than advanced economies, and uneven vaccination across economies could prolong border closures and delay the recovery of tourism-related industries. Second, as investor optimism is largely driven by the vaccine rollout, if the progress or effectiveness of vaccinations falls significantly short of expectations, the current capital inflows and the rebound in financial asset prices may come to an end. A sudden drop in capital inflows could trigger another wave of market turbulence. With the novel coronavirus successfully brought under control and a gradual recovery in consumption, the Mainland economy recovered rapidly in the second half of 2020. Meanwhile, benefiting from strong demand for pandemic-related products (such as medical equipment and high-tech products), exports also maintained growth (Chart 2.8). Throughout 2020, despite the unprecedented shock to the economy from the novel coronavirus pandemic, Mainland China's GDP still recorded a growth of 2.3%. Chart 2.8 Mainland China: Contribution of demand components to GDP growth Looking ahead, the latest consensus forecasts indicate that the Mainland economy will grow strongly by 8.4% in 2021, with private consumption expected to become the main driver of economic growth. However, whether the economic recovery can be sustained will still depend to a certain extent on the development of the pandemic. Although industrial production activities in the Mainland have normalized, the service sector remains partially disrupted as the pandemic has resurfaced in several northern provinces. Regarding the external environment, although exports resumed growth in the second half of 2020, global demand remains uncertain due to the outbreak of a new wave of the pandemic in most developed economies. In addition, Sino-US tensions may not ease in the short term, but the previously signed Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the concluded Comprehensive Agreement on Investment between China and the EU will help further integrate China with other economies, which may partially offset the adverse impact of Sino-US decoupling on the economic recovery. Considering that the economic outlook remains full of uncertainties, the government announced at the Central Economic Work Conference in December 2020 that the existing policy stance would not undergo major changes in 2021 in order to support economic growth, while also emphasizing the importance of controlling systemic risks, such as maintaining the stability of macro leverage and the sustainability of local government debt. Furthermore, the latest Government Work Report set the growth target for 2021 at over 6%. In the long run, the "14th Five-Year Plan" prioritizes technological self-reliance and the "dual circulation" strategy, with a view to raising per capita GDP to the level of moderately developed countries by 2035. The outbreak of the novel coronavirus seems to have had a limited impact on the repayment ability of bond-issuing enterprises, and the overall default rate in the Mainland bond market remained at a relatively low level in the second half of 2020. However, due to a sharp rise in bond defaults by state-owned enterprises, the total amount of defaulted bonds increased in 2020 (Chart 2.9). While the rise in state-owned enterprise defaults mainly reflects the central government's determination to break the "implicit guarantee" for state-owned enterprises to promote more rational market risk pricing, the limited fiscal space of some local governments may also be a contributing factor, especially for local governments in less developed regions. Chart 2.9 Mainland China: Scale and ratio of onshore bond defaults In the second half of 2020, financing costs for corporate issuers increased, especially for some high-risk issuers. Although the sustained economic recovery and the gradual normalization of interest rates led to higher financing costs for lower-rated issuers to a certain extent, several corporate default events occurred in the last quarter of 2020, causing credit spreads to widen significantly as a result (Chart 2.10). Chart 2.10 Mainland China: 5-year corporate bond yields Regarding the real estate market, Mainland property prices continued to rise in the second half of 2020, particularly in tier-1 cities. In contrast, the pace of property price increases in lower-tier cities was much slower (Chart 2.11). As for the housing oversupply problem that had plagued tier-3 cities in previous years, it was largely brought under control in 2020, partly because tier-3 cities recorded strong sales amid buoyant market sentiment. As of the end of 2020, the inventory-to-sales ratio in tier-3 cities remained at around 13 months, well below the peak of 31 months in early 2015.

Although real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) remained well below its pre-pandemic level, the Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 alongside a rebound in domestic demand and a further expansion in goods exports. With the hope that COVID-19 vaccinations will lead to a normalization of economic activities, the local economy is expected to resume growth in 2021, following the most severe contraction on record in 2020. However, the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, such as the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination takes time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in early 2021. Therefore, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure in the near term, while local inflation pressures will stay mild.  The Hong Kong economy improved in the second half of 2020 (Table 3.A), but economic activities remained well below pre-pandemic levels. The year-on-year decline in real GDP narrowed to 3.6% in the third quarter and further to 3.0% in the fourth quarter. For 2020 as a whole, however, real GDP fell by 6.1%, the largest decline on record, and marking the first time in history that it recorded two consecutive years of decline, following a 1.2% contraction in 2019. The latest GDP data by economic activity also showed that economic activities in the vast majority of sectors recorded year-on-year declines in recent quarters, with consumption- and tourism-related sectors contracting more severely than the overall economy.  On a quarter-to-quarter basis, real GDP started to rebound from the third quarter of 2020, ending the previous five consecutive quarters of decline (Table 3.A and Chart 3.1). Local private consumption resumed positive growth in the third and fourth quarters; however, consumer sentiment remained weak as the authorities re-imposed social distancing measures amid the local third and fourth waves of the pandemic. Overall investment expenditure also grew in the second half of the year alongside a brief improvement in business sentiment. Benefiting partly from a stronger export performance (especially exports to Mainland China), Hong Kong's merchandise trade expanded further (Chart 3.2). Trade in services remained weak as global tourism was still at a standstill. Overall, net imports (trade deficit) dragged down GDP in the second half of the year, partly reflecting a slower pace of rebound in goods exports compared to imports.  Chart 3.1 Real GDP growth and contributions of major expenditure components Chart 3.2 Real imports and exports  To cope with the ongoing pandemic, the Government launched two more rounds (the third and fourth rounds) of the Anti-epidemic Fund totaling $30.4 billion between September and December 2020 to help pandemic-affected sectors and citizens, and to enhance Hong Kong's anti-epidemic capabilities. The Government also announced additional counter-cyclical measures in the latest 2021/22 Budget to boost the economy, including a one-off issue of $5,000 electronic consumption vouchers and the provision of a 100% Personal Concessionary Guarantee Scheme for unemployed persons. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA), together with the Banking Sector SME Lending Coordination Mechanism, also announced in March 2021 that the Pre-approved Principal Payment Holiday Scheme would be further extended to October of the same year, and announced the extension of the repayment period for trade finance loans under the Scheme. These extension measures are expected to help alleviate the cash flow difficulties faced by some corporate customers.  With COVID-19 vaccines expected to bring economic activities back to normal, the Hong Kong economy is projected to resume positive growth in 2021 (for the year as a whole), but the strength and pace of the economic recovery are subject to numerous uncertainties, such as the development of the pandemic and the progress and effectiveness of the vaccine rollout. Given that widespread vaccination takes time, the local economy will still face significant challenges in the early part of 2021. On the external front, the Mainland economy is expected to strengthen further, providing support for Hong Kong's exports of goods and services, while the pace of recovery in other major economies will depend on the effectiveness of their mass vaccination programs, thereby affecting Hong Kong's merchandise trade and inbound tourism. The Government forecasts real GDP growth for 2021 as a whole to be between 3.5% and 5.5%, while the growth forecasts by international organizations and private sector analysts average 4.4%.  Labor market conditions deteriorated further in the second half of 2020 and early 2021. The seasonally adjusted unemployment rate climbed further to 7.2% in February 2021, a 17-year high (Chart 3.3). The underemployment rate also rose to 4.0%, a post-SARS high. Total employment stabilized after falling to a low level (Chart 3.3), while Government figures showed a continued decline in the number of job vacancies. The nominal index of payroll per person engaged, which reflects labor income, saw its growth slow to 2.0% in the third quarter of 2020, the lowest in nearly 11 years. To cope with the continuously deteriorating labor market conditions, the Government launched the Employment Support Scheme (ESS) under the second round of the Anti-epidemic Fund, providing time-limited (June to November 2020) wage subsidies to employers to help them retain employees. Following the end of the ESS, the Government introduced other targeted measures (such as one-off grants) under the third and fourth rounds of the Anti-epidemic Fund to further support sectors hard-hit by the pandemic. In the near term, the labor market is expected to remain under pressure due to weak economic conditions. Box 2 explores the potential impact of the boom and bust of inbound tourism on the local labor market.  Chart 3.3 Labor market conditions Chart 3.4 Different indicators reflecting consumer price inflation  Local inflation pressures continued to ease during the eight months from mid-2020 to February 2021. The underlying consumer price inflation rate fell significantly to 0.3% and 0.2% year-on-year in the third and fourth quarters of 2020 respectively, and further dropped to -0.5% and -0.1% in January and February 2021 respectively (Chart 3.4). The annualized 3-month rate of underlying inflation, which reflects inflation momentum, remained at a low level despite slight fluctuations in recent months. Specifically, price pressures on basic food eased, and the cost of meals bought away from home decreased noticeably, reflecting more restaurants offering takeaway discounts during the period of restricted dine-in services. Price pressures on other tradable goods (such as durable goods) remained moderate. On the services front, the rental component of the Composite Consumer Price Index (Composite CPI) remained soft alongside the consolidation of private housing rentals (Chart 3.5). Labor cost pressures also moderated in recent quarters (Chart 3.6).  Chart 3.5 Composite CPI rental component and market rentals Chart 3.6 Unit labor costs  As global and local economic conditions remain challenging, local inflation pressures should stay mild in the near term. In particular, local inflation will continue to be contained by the slower growth in newly signed private housing rentals earlier. Market consensus forecasts the headline inflation rate for 2021 to be at a moderate level of 1.4%, while the Government forecasts the underlying inflation rate and headline inflation rate for 2021 to be 1% and 1.6% respectively.  As the COVID-19 pandemic raged, inbound tourism quickly fell into a depression, raising market concerns that this crisis would cause scarring effects on the future recovery of the labor market. To this end, this Box empirically analyzes the impact of the inbound tourism boom on the local labor market, thereby exploring the potential implications of the current tourism depression.  Since 2000, inbound tourism has experienced significant booms and busts (Chart B2.1). Specifically, the number of visitor arrivals declined during the SARS (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) epidemic in 2003. Following the launch of the Individual Visit Scheme (IVS) in July of the same year, the number of visitors began to surge. Under the initial IVS, Mainland residents could apply in their individual capacity to visit Hong Kong once or twice a year, staying for no more than 7 days per visit. The IVS was expanded from April 2009 to allow eligible residents with Shenzhen household registration to apply for multiple-entry IVS endorsements (multiple-entry permit) valid for one year. Since then, the number of Mainland visitors has increased substantially. Driven by new cross-boundary infrastructure connecting to Mainland China, the number of visitor arrivals reached a record high between late 2018 and early 2019. Subsequent local social incidents halved the number of visitors in the second half of 2019, and amid the COVID-19 pandemic, inbound tourism has been at a standstill since late January 2020.  Chart B2.1 Visitor arrivals and related policies  Using the tourism boom brought about by the IVS as an example, we explore the impact of inbound tourism on local employment and income. We consider the introduction of the IVS in 2003 to be akin to a random economic shock, as it was nearly exogenous in timing and its launch could not have been anticipated by Hong Kong citizens. Our main analytical data are drawn from demographic data in the Hong Kong Population Census or By-census. Specifically, we use the 5% sample datasets from the 1996, 2001, 2006, 2011, and 2016 Population Censuses or By-censuses. In addition, we define tourism-related sectors as the food and beverage, retail, hotel, and transportation sectors.  First, we adopt a "difference-in-differences" analytical framework to compare the differences in employment outcomes before and after the implementation of the IVS between younger workers (aged 20-40) in the "treatment group" and older workers (aged 41-65) in the "comparison group". We assign the younger cohort to the "treatment group" because they are still in the early stages of their careers and can more flexibly make significant changes to their employment choices in response to the exogenous growth of inbound tourism. Since the labor market impact of the tourism boom brought about by the IVS may change over time, we also employ an "event study" approach to identify time-varying effects. Our empirical findings show that, compared to the older cohort, younger workers (especially females and those with only secondary education) were more likely to join tourism-related sectors following the implementation of the IVS. Among them, the impact of the IVS on the probability of young females working in tourism-related sectors was particularly significant and persistent, remaining at a level of nearly 5 percentage points (in terms of the average difference in the probability of entry compared to the older cohort) since 2006 (Chart B2.2).  We also use a similar approach to compare the incomes of those working in tourism-related sectors (treatment group) and non-tourism-related sectors (comparison group). Estimation results show that after the implementation of the IVS, the income growth of workers in tourism-related sectors was higher than that of employees in non-tourism-related sectors. Furthermore, compared to similar employees in other sectors, female workers and less-educated workers in tourism-related sectors experienced even higher and upward-trending income growth (3-20 percentage points) (Chart B2.3).  Chart B2.2 Impact of the IVS on female employment Chart B2.3 Impact of the IVS on the income of female and less-educated workers  The above results are broadly in line with international experience, revealing that tourism is an important source of employment, especially for young people, females, and less-educated workers. In the case of Hong Kong, our findings are also consistent with previous analytical results, namely that the strong growth of inbound tourism increased the market demand for lower-skilled workers, improving the robustness of the labor market for the lower-skilled segment. As inbound tourism plunges from boom to bust, these groups of workers may be more severely affected and warrant close monitoring.

The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate continued to stay close to the Strong-side Convertibility Undertaking (CU) level, and the Strong-side CU was triggered multiple times between September and October 2020. The strong demand for the Hong Kong dollar was mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that from buoyant IPO fund-raising activities and Southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect. As the Aggregate Balance increased to over HK$450 billion, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rates (HIBORs) softened across the board. Although uncertainties related to the development of the COVID-19 pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the ongoing tensions in Sino-US relations may exacerbate the volatility of capital flows, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, making it capable of withstanding the pressures brought by volatile capital flows. The Hong Kong dollar exchange rate stayed close to the Strong-side CU level, mainly driven by equity-related funding demand, including that from buoyant IPO fund-raising activities and Southbound capital inflows through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.1). Although some of the funds raised from IPOs were remitted away, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate traded within a narrow range between 7.7505 and 7.7544 in November and December, due to the improved sentiment in the local stock market and market expectations of increased funding demand towards the year-end. With fund-raising activities remaining active in the first two months of 2021 (Chart 4.2), the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate against the US dollar closed at 7.7568 on 26 February 2021. Overall, the trading of the Hong Kong dollar continued to be smooth and orderly. During the review period, the Strong-side CU was triggered multiple times, leading to an increase in the Aggregate Balance, which reflected substantial capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar. Between September and October 2020, the Strong-side CU was triggered 47 times. In accordance with the design of the Linked Exchange Rate System, the HKMA sold a total of HK$263.3 billion, causing the Aggregate Balance to increase from HK$193.1 billion at the end of August to HK$457.5 billion at the end of February (Chart 4.3). For the whole year of 2020, the Strong-side CU was triggered a total of 85 times, with cumulative inflows amounting to HK$383.5 billion. Analyzed from a cross-border perspective, total deposits increased, indicating no signs of significant capital outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest balance of payments figures showed that direct investment by non-residents continued to flow into Hong Kong in the fourth quarter of 2020, showing no signs of abnormal capital movements. Chart 4.1 Hong Kong dollar exchange rate Chart 4.2 Equity funds raised on the Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing Limited (HKEX) Chart 4.3 Aggregate Balance and Exchange Fund Bills and Notes During the review period, the Nominal Effective Exchange Rate Index (NEERI) of the Hong Kong dollar generally fell in tandem with the softening of the US dollar against major currencies (Chart 4.4). As the inflation differential between Hong Kong and its trading partners was small and had a limited impact on the Real Effective Exchange Rate Index (REERI) of the Hong Kong dollar, the movement of the REERI broadly tracked that of the NEERI. Chart 4.4 Nominal and Real Effective Exchange Rates Looking ahead, uncertainties related to the development of the pandemic, the pace of economic recovery, and the ongoing tensions in Sino-US relations may exacerbate the volatility of capital flows. As an international financial centre, various fund-raising activities (such as IPOs) are conducted in Hong Kong, resulting in substantial capital flowing in and out of Hong Kong. On the one hand, such fund-raising activities can attract international investors to transfer funds to Hong Kong. On the other hand, the funds raised by listed companies may subsequently be transferred out of Hong Kong for business needs. Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, making it capable of withstanding the volatility of capital flows without compromising financial stability. Amid continuous capital inflows into the Hong Kong dollar, the local monetary environment remained accommodative in the second half of 2020 and in recent months. Over the eight months since the end of June 2020, the Hong Kong dollar Monetary Base expanded by 20.8% (Chart 4.5). Analyzed by its components, the increase in the Monetary Base during this period reflected the expansion of the Aggregate Balance driven by the multiple triggerings of the Strong-side CU. On the other hand, other components, including Certificates of Indebtedness, Government-issued currency notes and coins in circulation, and outstanding Exchange Fund Bills and Notes, remained relatively stable. Chart 4.5 Components of the Monetary Base During the review period, large-scale IPO fund-raising activities led to an increase in Hong Kong dollar deposits generated by IPO subscription loans, causing Hong Kong dollar broad money (HKD M3) and its Hong Kong dollar deposit component to rise significantly between July and October 2020 and in January 2021 (Chart 4.6). Following the conclusion of the IPO fund-raising activities and the repayment of IPO subscription loans by customers, Hong Kong dollar deposits and broad money returned to normal levels at the end of 2020. Entering January 2021, HKD M3 increased substantially again, mainly driven by large-scale IPO fund-raising activities in late January. Overall, during the seven-month period since the end of June, HKD M3 grew by 21.7%; excluding the impact of the IPO fund-raising activities in late January, HKD M3 grew moderately by 9.1%. Analyzed by counterpart assets and excluding IPO subscription loans, the growth in HKD M3 was mainly attributable to the increase in the Monetary Base driven by the triggering of the Strong-side CU (Chart 4.7). As a major component of HKD M3, Hong Kong dollar deposits rose by 22.9% during the same period; excluding the impact of the IPO fund-raising activities in late January, Hong Kong dollar deposits grew moderately by 9.1%. Although Hong Kong dollar time deposits recorded a decline due to low deposit interest rates, this was fully offset by the rapid growth in demand and savings deposits, which was partly driven by investment demand. Chart 4.6 Deposits with Authorized Institutions by Currency Chart 4.7 Changes in HKD M3 and Counterpart Assets Overall foreign currency deposits grew steadily by 3.6% during the seven-month period since the end of June. US dollar deposits edged down by 0.3%, partly reflecting the weakness of the US dollar, while other foreign currency deposits grew strongly by 15.5% during the same period, mainly reflecting an increase in Renminbi deposits. Overall, due to the short-term volatility in Hong Kong dollar deposits caused by IPO fund-raising activities, total deposits with Authorized Institutions rose significantly by 13.2% during the review period (Chart 4.6). Excluding the IPO fund-raising activities in late January, total deposits grew moderately by 6.4%. It should be noted that as monthly monetary statistics may be subject to volatility driven by various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities), these statistics should be interpreted with caution. With the increase in the Aggregate Balance, HIBORs generally remained at extremely low levels during the review period (Chart 4.8). Despite the large-scale IPO fund-raising activities in the second half of 2020, HIBORs did not experience significant volatility due to the abundant liquidity in the banking system. Overall, the local interbank market continued to function normally. Chart 4.8 Hong Kong Dollar and US Dollar Interbank Offered Rates The Hong Kong dollar yield curve broadly tracked the movement of the US dollar yield curve and steepened during the review period, with short-term bond yields declining and long-term bond yields rising (Chart 4.9). Compared to the end of June, the yield on 3-year Hong Kong Government Bonds edged down by 4 basis points to 0.23% at the end of February, while the yield on 10-year Hong Kong Government Bonds rose by 67 basis points to 1.30% during the same period. Chart 4.9 Government Bond Yields, Composite Interest Rate, and Average Interest Rate for New Mortgage Loans Hong Kong dollar interest rates at the retail level mainly declined in tandem with HIBORs. The Composite Interest Rate, which reflects the average cost of Hong Kong dollar funds for retail banks, fell further from 0.71% at the end of June to 0.23% at the end of February 2021 (Chart 4.9). Due to the lower funding costs, the average interest rate for new mortgage loans also dropped from 2.02% in June 2020 to 1.56% in January 2021, broadly tracking the movement of the 1-month HIBOR. On the other hand, the Best Lending Rates of retail banks remained unchanged during the review period, ranging between 5.00% and 5.50%. Under the Linked Exchange Rate System, Hong Kong dollar interest rates are influenced by US dollar interest rates. Given that US interest rates are expected to remain low for a prolonged period, Hong Kong dollar interest rates should continue to stay at low levels, with occasional fluctuations driven by capital market activities and seasonal liquidity demand. In the face of a highly uncertain macro-financial environment, the abundant liquidity in the banking system should provide sufficient buffers to maintain Hong Kong's monetary and financial stability. The exchange rates of offshore Renminbi (CNH) and onshore Renminbi (CNY) against the US dollar have strengthened since the end of May (Chart 4.10), broadly reflecting the better economic outlook of Mainland China compared to the rest of the world, as well as the weakness of the US dollar. FTSE Russell announced in late September the inclusion of Mainland government bonds in its World Government Bond Index, and the investment demand further supported the strengthening of the Renminbi. For most of the review period, the CNH exchange rate traded at a premium over the CNY exchange rate, with an average premium of about 100 pips in the fourth quarter, which remained moderate by historical standards. Chart 4.10 Onshore and Offshore Renminbi Exchange Rates During the review period, liquidity conditions in the offshore Renminbi interbank market remained stable. Although the overnight CNH HIBOR experienced brief fluctuations due to occasional Northbound remittance demand and seasonal liquidity demand towards the year-end, it remained below 4% for most of the time (Chart 4.11). The 3-month CNH HIBOR fell in late December in tandem with onshore Renminbi interest rates, and subsequently rose again in late January, partly due to tighter onshore liquidity and seasonal factors. Chart 4.11 Overnight and 3-Month CNH HIBOR Fixings In the second half of 2020, Hong Kong's offshore Renminbi liquidity pool continued its growth trend. Since the fourth quarter, the growth of Renminbi deposits has accelerated, reflecting to some extent the appreciation of the Renminbi and its higher interest rates relative to other currencies. Compared to the end of June 2020, the growth of Renminbi customer deposits and outstanding Certificates of Deposit (CDs) accelerated, reaching RMB 826.3 billion at the end of January 2021, representing an increase of 21.9% (Chart 4.12 and Table 4.A). Among them, Renminbi customer deposits grew by 24.7%, mainly driven by the strong growth in corporate customer deposits. On the other hand, outstanding CDs decreased by 25.0% during the same period. Chart 4.12 Renminbi Deposits and Certificates of Deposit in Hong Kong As for other Renminbi business, outstanding Renminbi loans declined by 2.4% to RMB 159.2 billion during the seven-month period since the end of June 2020. On the other hand, Renminbi trade settlement in Hong Kong continued to grow strongly. During the seven-month period from July 2020 to January 2021, the value of transactions handled by local banks amounted to RMB 3,769.5 billion, representing an increase of 16.7% compared to the same period last year. Among these transactions, the growth of remittances from Hong Kong to the Mainland was higher than that of remittances from the Mainland to Hong Kong (Chart 4.13). Hong Kong has a massive Renminbi liquidity pool, which is sufficient to continue supporting a large volume of Renminbi payments and financial transactions. For the whole year of 2020, the average daily turnover of the RMB Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system reached RMB 1,191.5 billion, compared to RMB 1,133.9 billion in 2019.

Due to the persistent economic recession caused by the recurring COVID-19 pandemic, coupled with the impact of a prolonged low-interest-rate environment, the profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong further declined in the second half of 2020, and asset quality also slightly deteriorated. Nevertheless, underpinned by their still-strong capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust. During the review period, to continue supporting the overall economy in tiding over the difficulties, the HKMA decided to extend multiple relief measures. Looking ahead, although the rollout of vaccines may raise hopes that the global pandemic could be brought under control and economic activities could resume, the pace of economic recovery remains uncertain. The aforementioned uncertainties and ongoing geopolitical tensions will be unfavorable to business activities and continue to pose challenges to the local banking sector. In particular, as the pandemic will weaken the repayment ability of corporates and households, the banking sector should continue to closely monitor the impact of relevant downside risk factors on its asset quality. In the second half of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 38.5% compared with the same period in 2019. Correspondingly, the return on assets dropped to 0.62% in the second half of 2020, compared to 1.13% in the same period of 2019 (Chart 5.1). The net interest margin of retail banks narrowed from 1.63% in the second half of 2019 to 1.01% in the same period of 2020 (Chart 5.2), causing a decrease in net interest income that more than offset the slight growth in non-interest income, leading to a decline in profitability. For the full year of 2020, the overall pre-tax operating profit of retail banks fell by 29.4%, and the return on assets declined from 1.19% in 2019 to 0.77%. Chart 5.1 Profitability of retail banks Chart 5.2 Net interest margin of retail banks Largely due to massive fund inflows driven by stock market activities, Hong Kong dollar liquidity became more abundant. The Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) softened further in the fourth quarter of 2020. Among them, the 3-month HIBOR fell by 43 basis points in the second half of the year to 0.35% at the end of 2020 (blue line in Chart 5.3). The movement of the Composite Interest Rate (an indicator measuring the average Hong Kong dollar funding costs of retail banks) was also broadly similar, dropping significantly from 0.71% at the end of June 2020 to 0.28% at the end of 2020 (green line in Chart 5.3). The decline in the Composite Interest Rate mainly reflected the decrease in interbank funding costs and the downward adjustments of time deposit rates by some major retail banks. Chart 5.3 Interest rates From a broader perspective, the average overall Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs of licensed banks in Hong Kong fell moderately by 53 basis points in the second half of 2020 (red line in Chart 5.4). Chart 5.4 Hong Kong dollar and US dollar funding costs and maturity of licensed banks Looking ahead, as the global low-interest-rate environment is highly likely to persist and continue to weigh on banks' net interest margin performance, the profitability outlook for the banking sector will remain challenging. Furthermore, although breakthroughs in vaccine development have boosted market optimism about the global economic outlook, the trajectory of economic recovery remains highly uncertain given the considerable uncertainties surrounding the distribution and efficacy of vaccines. The aforementioned risk factors will continue to affect the loan quality and profitability of the banking sector in the near term. The capitalization of the Hong Kong banking sector remained robust and well above the minimum international standards. The consolidated total capital ratio of locally incorporated Authorized Institutions (AIs) stood at 20.7% at the end of December 2020, higher than the international minimum requirement of 8% (Chart 5.5). The Tier 1 capital ratio was 18.7% during the period, of which 16.7% was Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital. In addition, the leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs remained at a robust level of 8.2% at the end of December 2020, exceeding the statutory minimum level of 3% (Chart 5.6). Chart 5.5 Capitalization of locally incorporated AIs Chart 5.6 Leverage ratio of locally incorporated AIs Measured by the "Liquidity Coverage Ratio" requirement under Basel III, the liquidity position of the banking sector remained robust during the review period. The average Liquidity Coverage Ratio of category 1 institutions was 155.1% in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.7), well above the statutory minimum requirement of 100%. During the same period, the average Liquidity Maintenance Ratio of category 2 institutions was 57.9%, also well above the statutory minimum requirement of 25%. Chart 5.7 Liquidity Coverage Ratio The latest ratio figures under the "Net Stable Funding Ratio" requirement also indicated that the funding positions of AIs were stable. The average Net Stable Funding Ratio of category 1 institutions and the average Core Funding Ratio of category 2A institutions remained at high levels of 138.6% and 139.5% respectively in the fourth quarter of 2020 (Chart 5.8), well above their statutory minimum requirements of 100% and 75% respectively. The abundant liquidity and robust funding positions of AIs indicate that the Hong Kong banking sector is capable of withstanding liquidity shocks. Chart 5.8 Net Stable Funding Ratio Customer deposits remained the major source of funding for AIs, reflecting that the banking system maintained a stable funding structure. At the end of 2020, the proportion of customer deposits to the total liabilities of all AIs hovered at 56.1%, similar to the level six months ago (Chart 5.9). Chart 5.9 Liability structure of all AIs As the total deposits of all AIs increased in the second half of 2020 while total loans decreased during the same period, the average loan-to-deposit ratio for all AIs across all currencies fell from 76.0% at the end of June 2020 to 72.3% at the end of 2020 (Chart 5.10). The increase in total deposits broadly reflected the growth in both Hong Kong dollar deposits and foreign currency deposits. Correspondingly, as of the end of 2020, the average Hong Kong dollar loan-to-deposit ratio and foreign currency loan-to-deposit ratio fell to 83.5% and 61.0% respectively, compared to 86.4% and 65.5% respectively six months ago. Chart 5.10 Average loan-to-deposit ratio of all AIs The interest rate risk exposure of locally incorporated licensed banks remained at a relatively low level in the fourth quarter of 2020. Assuming a shock of a 200-basis-point increase in Hong Kong dollar and US dollar interest rates, the potential decline in the economic value of interest rate positions of locally incorporated licensed banks was estimated to be equivalent to 1.41% of their total capital base at the end of December 2020 (Chart 5.11). However, for the full year of 2020, total credit of the banking sector still recorded positive growth, although the growth pace slowed significantly from 6.7% in 2019 to 1.2%. On a half-yearly basis, total loans and advances of all AIs, after growing by 3.0% in the first half of 2020, decreased by 1.8% in the second half (Chart 5.12). The decline in total loans was due to decreases in both domestic loans (including loans for use in Hong Kong and trade finance) and loans for use outside Hong Kong. Foreign currency loans, after surging by 10.6% in the first half of 2020, decreased by 4.5% in the second half, partly reflecting a decline in demand for US dollar loans as global liquidity conditions improved. The banking sector turned slightly more optimistic about the near-term credit demand outlook compared to six months ago. The HKMA's "Opinion Survey on Credit Condition Outlook" in December 2020 showed that the proportion of surveyed AIs expecting an increase in loan demand over the next three months rose to 37%, while the proportion expecting a decline in loan demand over the same period decreased to 13% (Table 5.A). As the pandemic adversely affected the repayment ability of households and corporates, the loan quality of banks deteriorated slightly, but remained robust by historical and international standards. In addition, the pace of deterioration in loan quality also slowed down in the second half of 2020. The total classified loan ratio of all AIs rose moderately from 0.79% six months ago to 0.9% at the end of 2020, while the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio of all AIs increased from 0.49% at the end of June 2020 to 0.57% at the end of 2020. For retail banks, the total classified loan ratio and the overdue and rescheduled loan ratio rose to 0.82% and 0.48% respectively (Chart 5.13).

Entering 2022, global economic performance was sluggish, but inflation pressures continued to intensify across various regions, especially in the US. Looking ahead, the global economic outlook faces significant uncertainties, including the risk of large-scale pandemic outbreaks, and if US inflation is more persistent and broad-based than expected, the pace of monetary policy tightening may exceed expectations. If the Federal Reserve tightens monetary policy significantly and causes global financial conditions to tighten, it will exert pressure on the recovery of more vulnerable emerging market economies. Recently, the outbreak of military conflict between Russia and Ukraine may bring significant impacts to the global economy through trade and financial channels, and complicate the global monetary policy outlook. During the review period, the Hong Kong dollar exchange rate softened, but trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, and there were no notable signs of fund outflows from the Hong Kong banking system. The COVID-19 pandemic caused a massive shock to global financial markets in March 2020. During this period of market turbulence, some open-ended funds suffered massive capital outflows (Chart B1.1), putting pressure on their liquidity management. Chart B1.1 Capital Outflows from Selected Open-Ended Funds During the March 2020 Episode In addition to investors' liquidity needs, another reason for the massive capital outflows could be investors adopting a "first-mover advantage" to redeem funds early, thereby avoiding the redemption costs that could spike under market stress. To curb capital outflows driven by the first-mover advantage, some open-ended funds employ swing pricing—a pricing rule for open-ended funds that reduces investors' first-mover advantage. Although many open-ended funds used swing pricing during this episode, there is no empirical research indicating whether swing pricing can effectively reduce outflows from open-ended funds. Against this background, this special topic conducts an empirical study to understand whether swing pricing was able to reduce capital outflows from open-ended funds during the March 2020 episode, thereby lowering their liquidity risks. In addition, this special topic will also identify factors that may limit the effectiveness of swing pricing during market stress. Based on these assessments, we will provide policy recommendations regarding financial stability. The first-mover advantage refers to investors redeeming ahead of other investors, thereby passing the redemption costs onto them. The first-mover advantage primarily exists in open-ended funds that adopt traditional pricing rules, where the subscription and redemption costs of the fund's investors (such as transaction costs arising from portfolio adjustments) are reflected in the open-ended fund's price after the transactions are executed. Under this pricing mechanism, investors who redeem their shares first do not have to bear these transaction costs. This creates an incentive for them to redeem funds early, especially when large redemption costs are expected. Therefore, during market stress, the first-mover advantage becomes more pronounced as redemption costs are expected to rise. This amplifies the redemption pressures and liquidity risks faced by open-ended funds.

Amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market and concerns over the normalization of US monetary policy, the Hong Kong dollar (HKD) exchange rate softened during the review period. Due to abundant HKD liquidity, the Hong Kong Interbank Offered Rate (HIBOR) continued to stay at low levels. Overall, trading in the HKD foreign exchange and money markets continued to be smooth and orderly. Looking ahead, although uncertainties surrounding US monetary policy, the pandemic, and escalating geopolitical tensions may exacerbate capital flow volatility, Hong Kong has ample foreign exchange reserves and a robust banking system, making it capable of withstanding the shocks brought by capital flow volatility. Overall, the HKD stayed on the strong half of the Convertibility Zone for most of the time, and trading continued to be smooth and orderly. Since September 2021, the HKD has gradually softened against the US dollar (USD) amid risk-averse sentiment in the local stock market (Chart 4.1). Although the HKD rebounded slightly in October 2021 due to improved market sentiment, its upward momentum subsequently lost steam, mainly driven by weak Southbound net buying through the Shanghai-Hong Kong Stock Connect and Shenzhen-Hong Kong Stock Connect (Chart 4.2), as well as market expectations of a stronger USD as the US Federal Reserve's monetary policy outlook turned more hawkish. During the review period, IPO fund-raising activities continued to provide support for the HKD (Chart 4.3). Total deposits grew moderately during the review period, and there were no notable signs of capital outflows from the local banking system. Meanwhile, the latest Balance of Payments figures showed that non-resident direct investment continued to flow into Hong Kong in the second half of 2021, and there were no signs of anomalies in cross-boundary capital flows. Given the narrow inflation differentials between Hong Kong and its trading partners, the HKD Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) index broadly tracked the movements of the NEER index. As USD interest rates rise, under the normal operation of the Linked Exchange Rate System (LERS), outflows of HKD funds (the speed and scale of which will depend on prevailing market conditions) may lead to a weaker HKD and trigger the weak-side Convertibility Undertaking. Hong Kong also has ample foreign exchange reserves and a sound banking system, making it capable of withstanding capital flow volatility without compromising financial stability.   During the review period, monetary conditions in Hong Kong remained accommodative. The HKD Monetary Base rose by 1.4% in the eight months since the end of June 2021, mainly driven by an increase in Certificates of Indebtedness. Reflecting the additional issuance of Exchange Fund Bills to meet banks' ongoing demand amid abundant liquidity in the banking system, Exchange Fund Bills and Notes (EFBNs) increased by HKD 119.7 billion to HKD 1,188.7 billion during the review period, and the Aggregate Balance (before Discount Window activities) correspondingly decreased by HKD 119.9 billion to HKD 337.6 billion (Chart 4.5). Meanwhile, government-issued currency notes and coins remained relatively stable. However, it should be noted that monetary statistics may be subject to volatility induced by various short-term factors (such as seasonal and IPO-related funding demand, as well as business and investment-related activities); therefore, it is more appropriate to observe longer-term trends. For the whole year of 2021, total deposits and HKD deposits grew by 4.6% and 1.4% respectively. Affected by seasonal liquidity demand towards the year-end, the overnight offshore RMB HIBOR experienced slight volatility in late December 2021, while the 3-month offshore RMB HIBOR remained relatively stable and hovered around 3% throughout the review period (Chart 4.8). Major global stock markets continued to rally in the fourth quarter of 2021, but have consolidated since January 2022 amid growing market concerns over the tightening stance of major central banks in advanced economies and the escalating conflict between Russia and Ukraine. The profitability of retail banks in Hong Kong declined in the second half of 2021. Backed by robust capital and liquidity positions, the Hong Kong banking sector remained resilient. During the period under review, to further assist the economy in tiding over the difficult period, the HKMA extended a number of support measures. Looking ahead, the rapid spread of the Omicron variant may pose a threat to the economic recovery, which, coupled with the risk of a faster-than-expected pace of US monetary policy normalization, will pose challenges to banks' credit risk management. Banks should remain vigilant and carefully assess the potential impact of the relevant risk factors on the asset quality of their loan portfolios.
